text: What is the purpose of Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is it really about fulfilling their father's wish or do they have some other motives?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In their first statement, they said they did not trust Mr Lee Hsien Loong's leadership.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does this mean they will not stop until Mr Lee Hsien Loong steps down?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If it is really the case, then it is against the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wish as well as Singaporeans' democratic right.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew once said that he sent his children to Chinese schools to instill traditional values in them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If he were alive, he would be very sad to see his children in discord and the country being ridiculed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I urge Mr Lee Hsien Yang, if he really wants to be a filial son, to settle the issue privately and not hurt his father's beloved Singapore anymore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, whoever started the trouble should end it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is one of the richest parts of the inheritance we have received from our founding generation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we lose our unity as a country, we will lose our name in this world, and we will lose everything.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is something I will always defend.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, it does grieve and anger me to see so much of our country's reputation and trust being squandered on a social media war, of all things.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If all this turns out to be nothing more than some personal game of brinksmanship being played rather than a genuine desire to improve our political process, then I think there will be many angry and hurt Singaporeans to reckon with.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because for us ordinary Singaporeans, be we supporters of the establishment or supporters of the Opposition, this is not about what is to happen to one house, this is about what we want to happen to the country we all call our home.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To us on the ground who care, this saga is not a cynical game of cards.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is all our lives, not just one family's, but all of ours.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The worst of the allegations, which are not related to the house, are presently light on details, but because of the background and well-respected name of the accusers, the allegations have to be given their due weight.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If the allegations are true, the accused must be held to account.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If the allegations are false, the accuser must be equally held to account.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, how are we, the people, to make sense of those who are less powerful who have been sued or bankrupted for equally or less defamatory remarks?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For many conservative Asians, in the case of family, we will always want to protect our own.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I personally would rather never close the option of mercy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Should there still be the slightest possibility for mediation and grace and forgiveness to still intercede in this situation, and allow reconciliation and compromise to be made somehow, I hope it can be taken.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The difficulty here though is that because of the seriousness of the allegations of corruption, this situation can no longer be judged according to our personal preference or seen as just a domestic family quarrel.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a national level political issue and I respect the Prime Minister for recognising it as so by opening himself up to Parliamentary scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We pride ourselves as a country that governs by rule of law, so justice must be seen to be served.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We, the people, cannot be asked to tolerate a situation where the powerful are allowed to say or do whatever they wish, not be held accountable for it and then freely exercise their option to leave the country behind for greener pastures when they are done with their personal agendas.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is not the Singapore we want to live in.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Or the Singapore we have been asked to fight for.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because if investigations reveal there are truth and substance to the allegations, their wrongs must be made right.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is presently hard to ask more questions because, so far, details are just so vague and the people who can supply more detailed evidence to these questions are just not in this room.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Minister has shared his hope that "this full, public airing in Parliament will dispel any doubts that have been planted and strengthen confidence in our institutions and our system of government." I hope so much for that to be true, too, but from what I know of ground sentiments, I do not think that is going to happen for those who are unconverted or those who are sitting on the fence.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A Committee of Inquiry or Select Committee with enough independent non-PAP, non-subordinate representatives would help to address some of his accuser's concerns.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I understand this is not a process to be taken lightly and runs the risk of stretching out the painful saga, but I believe it is a significant display of political courage that will shore up much trust in our system's integrity, and it will also be a significant display of trust also in the people who will be asked to sit on those Committees.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister, I respect your decision to put forth your perspective on the Oxley issue as a statutory declaration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It means high stakes for you if you are found to be falsifying your statement.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, it does show me how seriously you have considered the stakes of your words.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I also respect your decision to open this up to Parliamentary debate and inviting all of us in this House to ask questions that call you to account because every word will go down on public record in the Hansard.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Your earlier sharing that you intend to put your words out in public, free of Parliamentary privilege, is an important move that I believe will build trust.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because in this culture right now shaped by social media, where words are allowed to flow fast and free, it has become all too easy to forget why things like statutory declarations and Hansards matter.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They remind us that for society to be strong, for democracy to be resilient, we must all allow the law to call us to account for our words, the things we choose to say, the things we choose not to say, because words are the way we build or break our worlds.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Beneath all this is the uncomfortable accusation about whether we are a country of one-man rule.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Part of the reason why perceptions of authoritarianism continue to fester is that there are still many people who believe and perceive the Government to be opaque in its decision-making and defensive in its communication about its work.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is just a long-standing perspective on the ground that is clear to anyone who looks at contentious Facebook comment threads on any socio-political issues.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The idea that anyone would see secret Ministerial Committees as nefarious may seem strange and even silly to those in Government who are familiar with what they are.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But to someone hearing about it for the first time, it can be construed to sound mysterious and Orwellian.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Where there is no information and understanding given, misinformation and misunderstanding will rush in to fill the vacuum.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This Oxley Road saga is painful but there are many thoughtful commenters who do not think this is necessarily a bad thing.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If anything, a deeper and more open conversation about how political power works in Singapore may be just what our system needs to truly grow up as a post-Lee Kuan Yew democracy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our electorate needs better political education, and more open, empathetic communication about our political processes can help.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is bigger than Lee Kuan Yew's values.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For no matter how great or powerful or righteous any one man may be, the best of men still die and a country must learn to live beyond them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think that is an offensive thing to say because that is a view Mr Lee himself has held.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: His expressed distaste for idolisation and personal monuments is something establishment and non-establishment Singaporeans can respect and get behind.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If Singapore is to stay strong, we must remember this to be true.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are a country of many people, many families and many interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have been serving on the Founder's Memorial Committee since 2015.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We have been gathering views from thousands of Singaporeans − historians, architects, regular people on the street, young people − about what kind of memorial would best honour the legacy of our Founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew and the pioneering team of leaders that built the nation alongside him.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What we learnt is that many Singaporeans wanted a memorial that could go beyond a mere recollection of the past.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They wanted a memorial to be forward-looking and ever relevant to a new generation, a memorial that did not just centre on one particular personality but powerful principles that could be passed on to endure forever.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many hoped for the Founder's Memorial, whenever and wherever it does get built, to ultimately stand for unity across the divides.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine whatever Singaporeans had wanted for the Founders' Memorial, they would want for the Oxley house as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Whether Oxley stays or goes or becomes a memorial garden with a basement, I hope we can find some compromise that will enable it to not go down in our history as a memorial born first in bitterness.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, hopefully that can be the beginning of some common ground that will move us all forward.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many Singaporeans in the process also referred again and again to the national pledge written by our founders as still the best representation of the story they wanted Singapore to live out, from generation to generation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore was, is and must always be about more than one man's − or one family's − values.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Even the national pledge that most closely enshrines all our nation's values was not written by one man alone.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It went through a long chain of drafting starting from a Mr Phillip Liau, Mr George Thomson, then Mr S Rajaratnam, various Ministry officials and then Mr Lee Kuan Yew and then submitted to the then Cabinet for final approval.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have come to believe that nations are really just families writ large.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Psychologists who study resilience in families notice that the more children know about their family history, the stronger their sense of personal agency, self-confidence and capacity to face challenges.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It also turns out that the pattern of the story told by each family matters.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some families tell their children an ascending narrative with a constantly upward, upbeat, hopeful trajectory.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some families tell descending narratives with a constantly downward depressing and pessimistic trend.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They understand that highs and lows were part of life and problems were better faced together rather than apart.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, yes, I know many Singaporeans are deeply saddened by all that has happened so far.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This season in our political history need not be part of a descending narrative but an oscillating one.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.15 pm until 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We see new Facebook posts and statements every other day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans are unsure of what to make of this debate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We want to know what is at the heart of this disagreement because some things just do not add up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, Mr Lee Hsien Yang shared that Dr Lee Wei Ling will probably stay in the house for many more decades.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Government also confirmed that, if this is the case, the current Cabinet, minus the Prime Minister, would likely not be the ones making the final decision.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, both sides agree that the decision could be decades away.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Should not Mr Lee Hsien Yang, or those after him, raise the issue with the future government and the people of Singapore at that point?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, Deputy Prime Minister Teo mentioned the possibility of a memorial park with only the basement preserved.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And recently, Mr Lee Hsien Yang suggested planting a memorial garden after the demolition of the house.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Why can both sides not continue to talk and come to an agreement over time?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, both sides have stressed that the Government has the right to gazette the house, because the Government has the responsibility of determining what is national interest.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This means that both sides cherish the core Singaporean principles: that the rule of law must apply; that no one is above the law; and that the law must serve the people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, are both sides really that far apart that a family dispute needs to be aired on the national stage with profound implications on Singapore's international standing and at a time of many pressing challenges?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We have heard the viewpoint of Mr Lee Hsien Yang, his wife and Dr Lee Wei Ling.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Having listened to the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister, it is clear that there is nothing to argue about the house.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The house and what to do about it cannot possibly be the reason why the siblings have gone public, since the Government has already said that there is nothing for the Government to do for many years, so long as Dr Lee Wei Ling continues to stay there.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Is it attacking the Prime Minister by using the house as a proxy?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang said he wants the Prime Minister down.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I note that over the last few weeks, Mr Lee Hsien Yang has evolved his position on what to do with 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Initially, he had stated that he had not thought through the plans beyond demolition.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Subsequently, he mentioned the possibility of planting a memorial garden.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And in his Facebook post yesterday, he stated that he has no current intention of redeveloping 38 Oxley Road as a luxury condo because it would be an affront to the values of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, a careful reading of his statement shows that this may not be definitive, because his declaration of "not inclined to apply for rezoning" does not rule out redevelopment under all circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, it is important for Singaporeans to be fully informed of the financial implications of various options for 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The public debate on what to do with the house will likely last a long time, perhaps even lasting beyond those currently involved.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is important for us to put all the facts on the table, including the financial implications, so that from now to the point of decision, Singaporeans can have a fuller appreciation of what drives the various viewpoints.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to ask about the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Most Singaporeans I speak to understand that Ministerial Committees are part and parcel of routine Ministerial work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, they can be fully reassured if they have a clear understanding of how this Ministerial Committee works and how it is organised to be exploring independently the options.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, who selected the members of the Ministerial Committee?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Was it the Prime Minister, Deputy Prime Minister Teo or somebody else?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, were discussion and information shared on a need-to-know basis within the Committee?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any other operating protocols that the Ministerial Committee will abide by in the future that would provide us with additional reassurances?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Much has been said about the seventh and final will.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Prime Minister share comprehensively why he did not contest the seventh will?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Last, I hope that Singapore can move beyond this issue after this Parliamentary debate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that the Government has chosen to respond to allegations through transparency and debate, because having a clean and honest government is what kept Singapore exceptional.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, Singaporeans want an immediate and firm reassurance that our Government integrity is beyond reproach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans hope that all parties concerned, especially after the debate today, will try to prevent their private debate from continuing to spill over to the public arena.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans want our Government's undivided attention on pressing national matters concerning the livelihood and security of our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The issues that directly affect Singaporeans' lives must always come first.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ruling party has thus single-handedly shaped the political culture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our political culture is one that does not condone any allegations of wrongdoing or impropriety against the Government of the day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Accusers are expected to back up their claims with evidence and, if they cannot, they are sued.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, Opposition politicians have been challenged to sue PAP MPs if they feel wronged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans have been sued for defamation for much less, one of the most famed examples being former MP Mr JB Jeyaratnam's utterance of the following at an election rally in 1997 where he said, and I quote, "Mr Tang Liang Hong has just placed before me two reports he has made to the Police against, you know, Mr Goh Chok Tong and his team." When it was suggested to the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew by a reporter that it was tenuous to base a defamation suit on Mr Jeyaratnam showing copies of Mr Tang's Police reports to a rally crowd, Mr Lee said this was a matter for the Courts to decide, and that his lawyers had advised him to sue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for Mr Jeyaratnam's offer to apologise without paying damages, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew was quoted as saying, "I'll leave things to the lawyers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have other things to do." In the normal course of events, the Government would do precisely that − leave the matter to be settled by lawyers in Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling would expect to face multiple defamation lawsuits for alleging that the Prime Minister has either lied or been corrupt in his dealings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As this has not happened and in view of the political culture that I have spoken of, there are Singaporeans who believe that the allegations made against the Prime Minister may have more than a grain of truth to them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many allegations have been made, and one need only peruse the document made public by Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling, released on 14 June 2017 titled, "What has happened to Lee Kuan Yew's values?" to remind themselves of them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would expect the Prime Minister to make a compelling case today and when this debate closes, but until Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling are fully heard, doubts will continue to linger and this matter will not be put to rest unless a resolution is sought through the Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Until that is done, who here would dare bet against a new Facebook post emerging from Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 1996, allegations were made against Mr Lee Hsien Loong during the Hotel Properties Limited (HPL) saga.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This episode erupted as a result of a public perception that both Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mr Lee Hsien Loong had unfairly received discounts in their purchase of properties from the developer HPL.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that case, a Parliamentary session, procedurally similar to the one we are having in the House today, was held to clear the air over the matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the circumstances and facts of that episode and how it came to be debated in Parliament were diametrically different in a number of important ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was also market talk that Mr Lee had been offered units in all the properties developed by the HPL group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister duly reported this to the then Prime Minister Mr Goh Chok Tong who ordered an investigation to get the Stock Exchange to provide a list of purchasers of two HPL developments, including questioning both the Senior Minister and then Deputy Prime Minister Mr Lee Hsien Loong, who had also purchased two HPL apartments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This fact was crucial, as a transparent caveat lodgment did not suggest wrongdoing by any stretch.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, Mr Lee Kuan Yew instructed Mr Ong Beng Seng, the Managing Director of HPL and a key player in clearing the air, to confront the media about the propriety of the purchases by himself and the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Lee stressed to Mr Ong that it was not enough for HPL to release a press statement but that a press conference was in order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Contrast this important detail with the absence of any sense of closure on the allegations made by Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling in the matter we are debating before the House today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The extent of probity and the affirmative conclusions to various matters in the HPL issue notwithstanding, by the time it came to an end in this House, MPs were in a position to triangulate various facts which, in totality, made it absolutely clear that no improprieties could be alleged by any reasonable person in the purchase of apartments by the Senior Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the matter before us today, can we honestly say that we are apprised and fully aware of the evidence and facts relevant to the allegations of the Prime Minister abusing his power so as to come to the same conclusion?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Frankly, by the end of today's debate, Iike the MPs in this House in 1996, if we can say yes, then there should no lingering suspicions or doubts that the Prime Minister abused his powers in the matter of 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that would be a welcome outcome for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, in view of the highly unusual decision by the Prime Minister not to clear his name in the Courts, the key question before this House is how do we move forward from here?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parliament can be a platform to look into and address the matter, but the choice of the appropriate Parliamentary forum is crucial.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, allegations of abuse of power by the Prime Minister may conceivably gain even more traction if the wrong Parliamentary forum is chosen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans are unaware that the consequence of ignoring a summons from Parliament are severe and a defaulter can be arrested and brought before the Select Committee to set the record straight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should any witness be contemptuous before the Committee, beyond hefty fines, Parliament is even empowered to commit that individual to prison for the rest of this Parliamentary term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Like many Singaporeans, I agree that the matters surrounding the will and, like disagreements, are fundamentally family issues and should be privately resolved forthwith either through the Courts or through mediation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it is the allegations of abuse of power that have to be decisively addressed, otherwise an odour will linger, one that will have severe and significant repercussions for Singapore's reputation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not believe a Parliamentary debate like the one we are having today will put the matter to rest, even as I hope I am wrong.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans are used to seeing Singapore being cited for our reputation for good governance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the last three weeks, what we have experienced is quite the opposite.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In fact, it is like a bad dream.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As one of my constituents had put it, I quote, "The reputation of Singapore is at stake here and all eyes from the international community are on us".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it is imperative that it must be put right.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad that he has apologised to Singaporeans but, as we all know, damage has been done to the reputation of Singapore and the confidence of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while we would have preferred not to have to discuss this in Parliament, given the serious allegations and how things have played out, it is important that we address the crux of the concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To be clear, the dispute between Mr Lee Kuan Yew's children is not what we are here to debate, as this is a matter to be settled between the siblings privately.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What I wish to speak about today are the consequential impact of the allegation of the abuse of power and, hence, the question on the integrity of the Singapore Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The matter regarding 38 Oxley Road is unprecedented.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It was in that very house that much of the foundations of Singapore's political history started.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The owner of the house was not just any person but Mr Lee Kuan Yew, one of Singapore's founding fathers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, the decision on what is to happen to the house on 38 Oxley Road is not a simple decision.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It involves not only the interest of Singapore but also the desire to honour Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his last wishes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is because of the unprecedented nature of the matter that "how" the decision is arrived at is as important as the decision itself.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, it is critical that as much information as possible on the process and rationale for the options being considered be shared with Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know we have a reputation of being efficient, effective, handling things in the best possible way with the least amount of disturbance and resources.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I think this is unprecedented and it matters to Singaporeans, not just because it is about Mr Lee Kuan Yew but it is also because it is about the history of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, we have to share as much information about the "how" as it is about the decision.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, this brings me to the question of the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The options that the Ministerial Committee arrives at will guide the decision that Cabinet and the government of the day will have to make when the time comes for a decision on 38 Oxley Road, when Dr Lee Wei Ling no longer lives there.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is, therefore, crucial that Singaporeans − and I stress this again, I know some people may say it does not matter because if we have the right people in the Committee it is okay, but it does matter – are given as much information on the process and the considerations made to arrive at the options.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will help assure Singaporeans if there is, indeed, independence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You have provided information to the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think it is also important for you to share the significance of you providing the Ministerial Committee with the statutory declaration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do not think people understand the seriousness, or at least not everybody may understand the seriousness of a statutory declaration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think it is important that you share its significance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One is, if there is no substance to these allegations, why are we spending our time in Parliament dealing with what is essentially a private family matter?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The other is that there is potential substance but this needs to be better dealt with somewhere else.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Two weeks have passed since the first allegations were made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Can you imagine that this would have been resolved in the Courts in two weeks?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Can you imagine that a special Select Committee could have been constituted, could have called witnesses, analysed the problem, submitted a report in two weeks?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is ridiculous to suggest that we cannot talk about this in Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have to talk about this in Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The first point, I find more interesting − that there are no specifics, there is no evidence, there is no substance to the allegations. "Do not let this go on, end this saga now, because there is nothing to it" − these are things that have been brought up by PAP MPs, Nominated MPs (NMPs) and Opposition MPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have not yet had specifics about what we should be doing differently, other than debate this in Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A special Select Committee is an instrument, a tool empowered by Parliament, as Mr Pritam Singh had argued just now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: How can he say that it would be better than Parliament, if he says that there is something wrong fundamentally with Parliament?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Yes, a special Select Committee has time, space and the opportunity to gather more evidence and to go into more details.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But it is given those powers by Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The expectations we have in Singapore are high.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The expectations of Parliamentary process, the expectations of prudence, of probity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But even on a very pragmatic basis, we are expected to forward plan just about everything.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If Members think back not many minutes, not many hours ago, to the Parliamentary Questions, I was standing at this very same rostrum, having to defend questions about the extent to which we could predict changes in our school landscape 15 years, 10 years, five years ahead of time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are expected to have drawer plans for just about every eventuality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When something goes wrong, when a conflict arises, when something is brought out into the public space, people are unhappy about it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One of the first questions that would be asked is, "Could you not have anticipated this?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Do you not have a scenario plan for this?" I suspect the social media posts and the subsequent storm of interest over the last two weeks were one of the few things that, perhaps, was not anticipated as a drawer plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But what to do with the property, the house, the heritage values, the conflicting public sentiments, surely, this is something that we need to have a drawer plan on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I want to make it very clear that what we are doing, this forward planning, this developing of scenarios, this consideration of public views and Opposition views, and diverse views, this is part of how our system works.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Coming to Parliament today is a demonstration that our system works, that our governance and our Government, the values and the expectations of our public are a marker of our system working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our ability to talk about this, the documents that have been shared here today, the record of conversations, the record of interactions that we have had that we bring to bear to make this debate happen, are a marker of the transparency and effectiveness of our system working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The allegations that are being put across, the mechanisms, a separation from the public and the private space, an attempt to moderate and deal with the influences, potential allegations of the abuse of power, these are markers and demonstrations of our system working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Everything we have done so far today, our ability to talk about this in this House, is a marker of our system working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is the form that many people are carried away with; but it is the substance that is far more appropriate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You can have a special Select Committee but if the Members on that special Select Committee do not do their job properly, it will not have the substance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We could have a debate here in Parliament but if we did not do our job properly, do our due diligence properly, search for questions, search for problems, search for evidence, search for substance to the allegations and bring them forth in this House, we would not be doing our job properly and we would not be giving substance to the form of a Parliamentary debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Singh's allegations that somehow this is an inappropriate place because MPs have not been able to bring up evidence, bring up substance to the allegations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is a marker of an absence of evidence, that is a marker of an absence of a problem, assuming the Members of the Opposition have been diligent about trying to find a problem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The words − the words of our Constitution, the words of our laws, the wording of clauses and paragraphs – they need to be turned into deeds, they need to be turned into deeds to demonstrate that we value them, that we value these processes and that we value this idea of accountability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Prime Minister has held himself up as an example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He set the bar very, very high but he has made it absolutely transparent what he expects of all of us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Recusal whenever there is the possibility of conflict of interests, a removal of any benefit that you might accrue to yourself, expose yourself to questioning, waiving of the Parliamentary privilege.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are steps to deal with conflicts of interest, deal with possible abuses of power and remove the possibility of conflict of interest, remove the possibility of an abuse of power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Yet, all of these mechanisms are now being criticised as markers of the exact opposite.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But it is of great interest that no one has been able to substantiate anything in this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One of the more serious allegations involves the issues to do with the AG, conflicts of interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I am going to leave it to some of my colleagues in the Ministry of Law to answer that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I just want to highlight a few of these.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin pointed out a few of these contradictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You want this thing to be settled quick, you want it to go to the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is only going to drag it out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You want this thing to be dealt with behind closed doors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Ministerial Committee operates behind closed doors; information is shared with the participants and the people that are called to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You want everything out in the public space for reasons of transparency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And yet, you are asking for us in this Parliamentary House to make a decision about a private act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You want to strengthen the standing of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When you stand up in this House, are you weakening it?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Are you generating confidence in the public sector and the public servants and the public sector officers who try to make the system work?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All of them have an understanding of what it means to separate the public and the private; this is part of their professionalism, their expectations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You want public transparency and yet you expect the Ministers cannot post on Facebook when allegations come in, when fake news come in, when misinformation comes in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are not allowed to post on Facebook to counter this?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We leave those allegations and misinformation and disinformation out there?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have to decide what it is we want out of this process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We all want for Singapore to be stronger and a big part of that is going to be taking a position on whether our system of governance, our system of Government and our Parliamentary democracy are correct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But the question is, do we have a system that can detect it, that can deal with it and to prevent it from happening again?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Are you trying to bring down this House?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You should stand by the values of this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You should accept that this is a good place and the right place to bring these issues out to have a debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If there are facts to substantiate these allegations, bring them here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And if it is appropriate, further action can and should be taken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: No one has been able to substantiate this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I also share Mr Low Thia Khiang's sentiments about the bright red line between the public and private space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is the essence of good Government and good governance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is exactly the key issue that the public and the private space must be separated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But everything we have heard so far is detail after detail, document after document, attempt after attempt, in order to achieve that separation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You can say it is separated but it is the actions and the deeds that you take in order to make that separation real, make yourself accountable, that are far more important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have had a detailed explanation of how the Prime Minister has done exactly that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I agree with Mr Low Thia Khiang's sentiment that we should end this now or as soon as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A suit is not going to end this now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I am sure it will come up in the headline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But how can you follow that up by asking for the saga to then be protracted by a whole bunch of other mechanisms?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Then, there will be a strong bright line.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Then, our system will be stronger and we can move on with our lives, and we can move on with all the other things that we need to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This process is ugly, it is disquieting, it is upsetting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If it was easy and if it was fun, it would not have to be brought here in Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I suppose Government is not there to just deal with the nice things.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Parliamentary debate, the idea of the contest that we have in our speeches and in our discussion that politics itself is contestable, that the issues brought before this House are to be contested over and that we must be rigorously applying ourselves to that contest in order to get the best possible outcome for the people that we serve and for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is an important part of what has got us here today, and what will take us forward and make us a resilient and stronger system to withstand any further shocks, allegations and problems that surface.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But that requires that we engage in this and that we believe that this contest is useful, that we believe that iron sharpens iron, that we believe that when we stand in this House, we are doing something worthwhile and not abrogating and abdicating our responsibility to somebody outside, that we are not elected by the people and throwing the problem back to the people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have to solve and make decisions and analyse the facts on their behalf and hold ourselves accountable to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Of course, the proverb is only half correct − Proverbs 27:17, "Iron sharpens iron, as man sharpens man".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, it is always inappropriate to quote a clause out of context or quote only half a paragraph.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Because if you try to sharpen iron against iron, both get blunted and a lot of heat is generated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In combination with the will of the people, we have to sharpen our iron against the will of the people and their expectations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But most importantly, we have to do so against our pride in ourselves as representatives of this Parliamentary democracy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our pride in ourselves as instruments of our democracy and our governance, we must try as hard as possible to contest this space, to do right by Singapore and by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And if having tried as hard as possible to find the problem, to find some fact, to find some weakness, there is none, then surely, we should acknowledge that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Surely, that is the service that we do to the values of this House and the values of Singapore and the issues before us that we have to provide some resolution to.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang, I would prefer clarifications to be taken after all the speeches, please.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's social compact under Lee Kuan Yew was − civil liberties may be curtailed, but in return your government will respect the rule of law and be utterly beyond reproach." And, indeed, Mr Lee Kuan Yew himself had also spoken many times on the rule of law in Singapore, and on how our laws reflect the traditional Asian value system which places the interests of the community over and above that of the individual.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, when he spoke at the Opening of the Singapore Academy of Law in 1990, he stated in the context of land acquisition that his Government puts communitarian interests over those of the individual.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: He added, "These were contrary to the rights of the individual upheld in English jurisprudence.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But because our people shared our values, they supported and abided by our legislation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government had failed to establish the basis for political stability and social cohesion, the rule of law would have become an empty slogan in a broken-back Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But we have succeeded, and the rule of law today in Singapore is no cliche." I quote Mr Lee again, "I am often accused of interfering in the private lives of citizens.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I did not, had I not done that, we wouldn't be here today.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I say without the slightest remorse, that we wouldn't be here, we wouldn't have made economic progress, if we had not intervened on very personal matters − who your neighbour is, how you live, the noise you make, how you spit, what language you use.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Never mind what the people think." The rule of law in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I repeat, "and I say it without the slightest remorse, that we would not be here, we would not have made economic progress, if we had not intervened in very personal matters − who your neighbour is, how you live, the noise you make, how you spit, what language you use".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I may add, do I get my house demolished or not?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Do I get buried where I choose to be buried?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Do we keep the Sungei Road Hawker Zone?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot imagine Mr Lee banging tables and insisting on the demolition of his house.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As one who upheld communitarian laws over the interests of individuals, I cannot imagine Mr Lee insisting that his individual interest must prevail over communitarian interests.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As one who defended his Government's land acquisition laws, I cannot imagine Mr Lee insisting that the Government cannot acquire his own property.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If in life he submitted himself to the rule of law, I cannot imagine him overruling it in death.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It remains to be seen as to why the demolition was drafted as a wish rather than a directive or a condition under his will.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot imagine Mr Lee wanting his will to prevail over that of the communal good.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot imagine Mr Lee wanting to be treated above how other citizens are treated.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, only those closest to him would know the answer.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I could just share a little personal experience.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In June 2015, when I was part of the Singapore delegation to the United Nations Convention for Rights of Persons with Disabilities in New York, I was one of the speakers for a Singapore side event on "Urbanisation and Disabilities".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I shared the Singapore story of transformation: from attap houses without proper sanitation facilities to high standard public housing with accessible features and universal designs; the transformation of our transportation infrastructure into an inclusive and accessible system, now the envy of many other countries; transformation of our underprivileged being provided education, opportunity, professional and social mobility.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I shared the transformation of our journey towards acceptance and inclusion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There were about 120 people in that room.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They were surprised at what we achieved, and they were inspired that we did it in 50 years.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I said there were three factors that were critical: political will, Civil Service buy-in and mutual trust between the public, people and private sectors.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Undergirding those three things are, in my view, at least three important co-dependent factors: the rule of law, political stability and economic progress.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Without any of the three, it could not have been possible for us to look after our people or nurture them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Were we not to uphold the rule of law, we would degenerate into political and civil infighting.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Were we not to uphold the rule of law, we would not see economic progress to support our social progress.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Were we to divert our efforts and our attention to political infighting, we could not have spared resources or attention to care for the underprivileged in our community, to care for our people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So much at stake and what are we doing today?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are here in Parliament debating serious allegations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have had so much to deal with − an economy undergoing disruption in Singapore, globally.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have just finished our Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) consultations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There are so many proposals to be implemented.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: At the national level, we have just finished our Third Enabling Masterplan.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So much to be done, so many people to look after − the health of the Pioneers, the health of our children − all these things.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How do we educate our young, how do we bring them up with the right values?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: On the personal level, we worry for our jobs, our own health, our children's future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We worry about safety, we worry about terrorism.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So much at stake, so much to be done, and we are here talking about whether certain allegations against the highest officers in the land are valid or not.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I doubt very much that a debate could resolve this issue.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In as much as we worry about what people think of us, we also need to realise that we ourselves must band together.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If people are looking at Singapore and laughing at us, this is the time for us to be together as a people because this is the time for us to show to others that we are not a people to be easily shaken, easily bullied.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I say that this is a time for us to embark on destruction.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let us be one people to destroy − to destroy the divide that splits us as a people; destroy the suspicion that we have towards one another; destroy the memories of unhappiness, of hatred; destroy even partisan differences.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is the time for us to band together and exercise grace and forgiveness; to remember tender moments, happy moments and to remember that that is what our founding fathers would have wanted for us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I say again, let us destroy the divide.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Prime Minister did not challenge the will and it was granted probate from the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many questioned what then is the role of the Ministerial Committee with regard to the will?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to Deputy Prime Minister Teo, and as he mentioned earlier, the Committee's interest in Mr Lee Kuan Yew's will is simply to help them understand his thoughts regarding the house.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many are confused as to what it is that requires further understanding, and does the Committee not accept the will as the official expression of Mr Lee's last wishes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no provision in this piece of legislation about taking advice from the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will evidence gathered and decisions taken by the Committee influence the processes set out in section 11?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister and NHB be in any way bound by opinions or findings by the Committee?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At this point, is NHB also concurrently studying about whether to preserve the house?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, as explained earlier, I understand the Committee is studying and listing options.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But would not the factors this Committee is using, including public sentiments, change in the future?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What then is the point of setting up this Committee now and making recommendations now?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Things would definitely change in two to three decades.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, can the Prime Minister or Deputy Prime Minister clarify whether the same emphasis was placed on other important buildings like the National Library?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There has been much talk on social media about this, and I suppose the question really is, how do we decide what to preserve or conserve and when do we set up Ministerial Committees for these decisions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about this earlier, but can I confirm if Ministerial Committees were set up for previous important buildings as well?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond all these questions, I appreciate that this is not an easy issue to resolve and definitely not one with straightforward answers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last Friday night, I had two meetings and this issue was brought up in our conversations in both meetings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the first meeting, the consensus was to demolish.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second meeting, the consensus was not to demolish.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They did not support demolishing the house as they felt we have so little heritage left in Singapore that we should preserve or conserve whatever heritage we have left.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, it is easy to understand why we should demolish.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is perhaps harder to understand why we should not demolish, and can the Deputy Prime Minister take this opportunity to further explain and provide details on what exactly is the heritage value and why an option to preserve or conserve the house should be considered?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It really is not an easy issue to resolve and, as such, I hope, like many Members of this House have suggested, that we set up a Select Committee to look into this and find a way forward.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am not even bothered why the current owner of 38 Oxley Road would want it demolished as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These are private matters for the Prime Minister to settle with his siblings and they do not concern the state.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I was not a bit affected by this issue until when other Ministers started to weigh in on the matters.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The whole episode then took a cringing turn, and allegations of abuse of power began to flow in.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Why are Ministers taking sides in a private dispute on a house that is still legally in the hands of a private individual?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In recent statements made by Ministers on social media, the fate of 38 Oxley Road seems to hinge on whether the house should be demolished completely according to the will of Mr Lee Kuan Yew or preserved, in whole or in part, as a political heritage.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One can easily infer from the tone set by these Ministers that the Government is tending towards the latter option, and that, sadly, will drag the Government into the picture to decide on the fate of 38 Oxley Road, in the guise of public interest.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some Ministers seemed to allude to the sanctity of the house from a historical context and that it deserves preservation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some Ministers had commented that many important meetings and critical decisions on the future of Singapore took place at 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While that is not a far-fetched statement since it is the birthplace of the only ruling political party in Singapore since 1965, what other roles did the house play in our march from Third World to First?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What official and history-making decisions and declarations affecting Singapore were made in the basement of this house, other than it had always been the private abode of Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mdm Kwa Geok Choo?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Did the Cabinet of the day hold its first post-1965 meeting at Oxley Road?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Did the Cabinet meet regularly at the house rather than at the old Parliament House or Istana?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One thing is very clear to me − a political party was founded in the basement dining room of 38 Oxley Road, not modern Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Modern Singapore was thrust into existence, not by its own free will, on 9 August 1965, under circumstances that are well documented in our history books, and 38 Oxley Road hardly gets a memorable mention anywhere.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As the Prime Minister has said earlier, this is just an old house.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Thirty-eight Oxley Road probably holds so much intimate and private memories for Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mdm Kwa Geok Choo that none of us in this Chamber, maybe with the exception of the Prime Minister, should even attempt to try to understand or question why they would want their house to be demolished immediately after they are gone.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Even if the balance of the fate of the house is tending towards preservation in the name of public interest, and the Prime Minister recuses himself in this matter, the buck still stops with him.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Surely, the Prime Minister is not a lame-duck commander-in-chief in this matter.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He has the power to have the final say, take the whole matter off the Government's hand and resolve it privately or in Court, as he should.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The surviving members of the Lee family should not outsource this decision to the Government or any secret committee.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The statement contains disturbing revelations and undisclosed facts and allegations of abuse of powers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The fact that the Prime Minister and our current AG had a commercial relationship was never publicly disclosed until now.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How long has Mr Lucien Wong been the personal lawyer for the Prime Minister?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While such a relationship may not allude to anything, a personal and commercial relation between the Prime Minister and the appointed AG should be publicly disclosed in the name of transparency.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When I sought the advice of someone from the charity sector about mundane disclosure, this person said, when in doubt, more disclosure is better than less.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Could the Prime Minister explain why the public disclosure of his relationship with the AG is not necessary?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Dr Lee Wei Ling wrote, and I quote: "Singapore has no such thing as the wife of the Prime Minister being a ‘first lady'.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Lee Kuan Yew was Prime Minister from 1959 to 1990.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: During those many years, his wife (our mother) consistently avoided the limelight, remaining his stalwart supporter and advisor in private.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: She lived discreetly and set a high bar for the conduct of a Prime Minister's wife.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: She would never instruct Permanent Secretaries or senior civil servants.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The contrast between her and Ho Ching could not be more stark.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While Ho Ching holds no elected or official position in the Government, her influence is pervasive and extends well beyond her job purview." Mr Lee Kuan Yew, in his own words about his relationship with his wife, said, "I made a point, however, not to discuss the formulation of policies with her, and she was scrupulous in not reading notes or faxes that were sensitive." From both accounts, Madam, it is a given that the wife of the Prime Minister, and for that matter, the wife of any Minister, would have easy access to information and the inner workings of the Government.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Prime Minister has said that it is the duty of the Minister to correct any abuse of power committed by their family members.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Nonetheless, these safeguards should be spelt out clearly so that the core values of the Civil Service would not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Surely, family members of Ministers and political appointees cannot act with impunity just because they are private individuals and the code of conduct only applies to public officeholders.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, what are the safeguards for the Civil Service if such family members decide to go beyond their call of duty for all the wrong reasons?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, what prompted Dr Lee Wei Ling to allege that the wife of the Prime Minister is throwing her weight around with the Civil Service?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What pervasive influence did she exert that are well beyond her job purview?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would NHB dare to ask the wife of the Prime Minister to show proof that the items on loan were obtained legally?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Between state agencies, did they not know that PMO does not have a contact person named "Ms Ho Ching"?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And what business did MCI have in photographing and cataloging a private house?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Was the Government working on a secret project?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These are allegations that need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In my dealings with the Civil Service, many civil servants are neutral and we must protect them from being put into positions of conflict against their values, personal and professional.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The choice lies with the family and not with this Government.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember one of my last conversations with my late father.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He was ill with cancer, not getting better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I was at his bedside visiting him at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: By then, he could not stand up for long.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And then he reminded me not to take up too much time with him.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because there were other cancer patients who needed me more as their doctor.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a story that every Singaporean family relates to in their own way, in their own journey, whether it is other doctors or nurses in our hospitals working to cure illness, to comfort patients, even if it means less time with loved ones who are sick.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a story that is lived by our teachers in our schools who uplift the lives of young Singaporeans, even though every extra hour at home with their own children would mean one less hour at school with the students they are looking after.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a story that will be understood by our Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) servicemen who know that operational readiness and commitment to defence, making that sacrifice is how we deter external threats from intimidating Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it is a story that will be known by our Home Team officers who leave their children behind when they go on duty − firefighters running towards danger rather than running away as we saw on videos on social media some months back; Police Officers stepping into harm's way so that other parents' children can live and sleep safe at night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
