text: Yet, I am sure many Singaporeans, and many of my residents have told me, they can only imagine how much harder it is for our Prime Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because while Mr Lee Hsien Loong has his family duty as the eldest son, Prime Minister Lee has a duty to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Putting Singapore first means a duty to uphold the rule of law.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because in a fair and just society, the system and laws have to be bigger than any one person or family because no one comes into this world choosing who their parents are, where they will be born, which postal code they will be born in.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is why the law must apply equally, regardless of your background.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the law of land acquisition does apply equally to the wealthy and famous, as much as to the farmer in a kampung.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This equality of land law is still something very, very rare throughout the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we look all around us, across the arc of human history, dispossession, being disadvantaged in the system, is often what happens to the powerless elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In other countries, curbs on private property rights very rarely hit those with power, or those who can influence people in power.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And that is why we have to preserve this Singapore principle of the rule of law.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My residents, many are not lawyers; they are lay persons.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They are wondering, could this task not have been assigned to the Founders Memorial Committee, which was already looking at how to remember our Founders?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could the question have been put to the Founders Memorial Committee earlier?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Like me, my residents are not legally trained.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: People ask, how does the Ministerial Committee fit in with a layperson's understanding of due process?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This needs to be explained thoroughly because the rule of law is not just about due process.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is about public confidence in that process, confidence that the rule of law applies and is applied equally, the confidence that allows people from all walks of life to believe in the system and continue living in it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew had written about Dr Lee Wei Ling continuing to stay at 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Right now, there does not seem to be a need to rush to decide.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, some of my residents asked: what exactly is being asked of the Government in this dispute?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Indeed, if 38 Oxley Road were demolished in haste, as Mr Png Eng Huat seems to allude to, it may well mean fewer choices for future governments and later generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is an issue of intergenerational equity here.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because once the house is smashed and gone, it is lost forever.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In SG100, two generations from now, SG100 Singaporeans might want it to stand again − the house or the basement.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we should not rush, especially when emotions are high and feelings are raw.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do not rush to tear down what cannot be rebuilt.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do not rush to unmake what can never be made whole again.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The same principle has to apply to the greater house that Mr Lee and the Founders built.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A greater house − the home that is Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our cohesion as one people, our togetherness, our system of rule of law, that fairness and our stature as a shining red dot, hoping to light the way to a better future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A country where citizens can stand tall in the world, proud of what our country stands for.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All this is the greater house that is Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our founding leaders, our Pioneer generation spent their whole lives building this up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Let us not allow it to be knocked down on a whim.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, the story is always about getting the country better and making the country even better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, if there is a problem, it matters whether there is evidence, because the evidence helps us find out where we can do better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But likewise, if there is no evidence, let it be known as well that there is no evidence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is the whole night tonight to post on Facebook.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure our PAP MPs will appreciate it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure our NMPs will appreciate it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure the people of Singapore will appreciate it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If there is evidence, let it all come out before this debate is over.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do not come back later and say there was no chance to have the issue heard, because there are many other things that Singapore needs to deal with − big, big challenges ahead for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met Singaporeans − brothers and sisters − in the Offshore and Marine sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know what the recent oil prices have done to that sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Husbands, fathers, mothers, breadwinners are wondering if they will still have a job next month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Have the recent events helped our brothers and sisters who are worrying about work?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At our Inclusive Job Fair in Clementi and during my home visits as a constituency MP, I have met middle-aged workers wondering if there will be new jobs available if they lose their existing jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has what happened online, has all that helped our workers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see terrorism and extremism around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS) wanting to set up a province, a wilayat in Southeast Asia, trying to brainwash people through social media from halfway around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has this public dispute, this poison, has it made us safer?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see world events shaping our environment, shifting the stage that Singapore balances on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does all this strengthen our place in the sun?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does it help our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) stand tall and proud overseas?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does it help our citizens when they seek opportunities elsewhere and engage with overseas counterparts?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or has it cast a long shadow on our little red dot?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each of us, in our own way, can shape the future for the sons and daughters of tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must always ask ourselves how we can make things better, so that our grandchildren's generation never find themselves wishing they could turn back the clock and start all over again.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: The Member said that I wanted the house to be demolished in a haste.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: So, which part of my speech did I say that?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: If I may ask, what is Mr Png's position on whether the house should be demolished, and whether he thinks it should be demolished now?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Actually, I would like Dr Tan to answer first.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: His apology was first made a few weeks ago, which was televised and broadcast to all Singaporeans to see, and it was made again today.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We live in an age, Mr Deputy Speaker, when some foreign world leaders make their rounds on talk shows, who use social media to insist that they have nothing to apologise for.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In politics, like in law, it is usually the case that to admit fault seems to many to be an invitation to be attacked in return.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But a genuine apology to the Government's first and foremost stakeholders − the people of Singapore − disarms.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: A genuine apology is a gesture of self-humbling, a willingness to be less powerful than one can be.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I must say, Mr Deputy Speaker, that what comes after an apology is equally, if not more, important.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Today's Parliamentary Sitting aims to set out and analyse truths, not about the validity or invalidity of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew's final will.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Our duty today is to identify and ask questions on behalf of our constituents or, if you are an NMP, our functional groups, regarding the origins of the allegations aired in public.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: These allegations have been inimical to Singapore's reputation, and I think they indicate, if nothing else, that the country's leader and his siblings do not speak with one voice.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There are two points I want to make, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The first is what process should we choose when we are discussing these questions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The fact that the Government endeavours to prioritise the common good that seeks to balance public against private interests, the long term against the short term is clear.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is the way that Singapore has been and, I hope, should always be governed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is also in keeping with our settled policymaking traditions, as our Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam has said recently.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But what about, as there is now, when there is a situation of real or apparent conflict, something that Deputy Prime Minister Teo mentioned earlier, which may be seen to be contrary to both Ministerial and Public Service codes of conduct?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's answer seems to be perhaps establish a Cabinet Committee and, of course, for the Prime Minister or whichever Cabinet Minister is involved to recuse themselves.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: However, even if there is no mystery to the Members of this House as to what Cabinet Committees are − there are Cabinet Committees, there are Cabinet subcommittees, there are Cabinet task forces − there is no mystery behind them, and it is not something that only Singapore has.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the United Kingdom, which is where we get our own traditions from, there are 10 Cabinet Committees, and there are about 15 Cabinet subcommittees.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But even in that grand nation, there has been a push to move away from Cabinet Committees for this precise reason of an allegation of secrecy.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister Theresa May disclosed the thematic focus as well as the membership of all her Cabinet Committees which are responsible for the day-to-day decisions made and which are designed to take the pressure off the full Cabinet meeting for every decision that has to be made.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But in special circumstances, such as this, which have animated the minds of so many Singaporeans, should we go beyond looking at Cabinet Committees?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The process of decision-making, Mr Deputy Speaker, and how this is communicated in the eyes of Singaporeans, are important.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That gives a sense that any questions that should be asked could be asked at an early stage.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Standing Order 101 also allows the Speaker, or her delegate, to serve as the Chairman of that particular Committee, even if the Speaker is not a Member of that Committee, giving one a sense of neutrality or independence.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we were to go further, where senior Cabinet Ministers may wish to, in good conscience, recuse themselves from the decision-making process, perhaps Parliament could study whatever mechanisms could be put in place.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We should certainly look to the future, as Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary mentioned earlier.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If you are looking 15 years into the future, or even further, should the processes also not be refined?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What happens if this were to recur again in a different Prime Minister's administration?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Can we count on so clearly that that Prime Minister would recuse himself or herself from the decision-making process?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Should there not be some form of check, some neutrality?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Someone who is independent of the Government and the Civil Service to be appointed in precisely this sort of situation, if nothing else, to insulate the Cabinet from an appearance of conflict.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When we look at the divide that has formed over what should be done over 38 Oxley Road, we notice a clear divide.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, members of the public from institutions or organisations, such as the Heritage Society, feel that acceding to an individual testator's wishes, whoever he or she may be, without undergoing the process administered by our local heritage and planning institutions, may establish an unwanted precedent for future preservation or conservation cases.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we do this now, what about the next case that comes up?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the course of the studies which Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned earlier − one study undertaken by NHB, and the other study undertaken by URA − looking at the possibility of preservation or conservation, where can we involve public consultation, where can we get the views of the public?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The opportunity for such consultation calls to mind a desire that was expressed during the Our Singapore Conversation dialogues a few years ago, where the report finally concluded that the Government should "share the reasons behind policies and create or enhance spaces for ongoing interactions".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It bears mention that people can become disenchanted if they feel that any information that they are providing is at the final stages of the process, that their consultation may be piecemeal.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear from our style of Government, from Singapore's style of Government, be it in foreign or domestic policy, be it with most important trade or investment issues, or with arts and culture, that one thing that cuts across all these areas – and I think it is deeply within our national psyche – is national heritage, what we think is important for our identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This genesis or heritage story that we have is at the heart of what is going on right now.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In this policymaking that we go for, when we think about the processes that we put in place and we also think about how to confront these sorts of disputes in future, what can we do to include Singaporeans in this process?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If heritage is so important to Singaporeans, and I am sure it is, from everything that we see, from all accounts, then that is the greater debate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, how would such subjective information on his wishes help the Committee in its deliberations to identify the options for the house?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think it trivialises what has happened today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have heard the Ministerial Statements made by the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister and robust questions have been posed to both of them and their Cabinet colleagues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have posed some of these questions and these questions are drawn from the allegations that were made by Mr Lee Hsien Yang as well as Dr Lee Wei Ling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fact that they are not here does not mean that the allegations they have made outside this House cannot be conveyed as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both PAP MPs as well as Opposition MPs have done the same thing, together with my colleagues who are NMPs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is disappointing to hear that they have already prejudged that the debate is pointless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think we have still not heard the answers from the Ministers, and such conclusions, being prematurely drawn, undermine the confidence in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This House is definitely more important than the house at 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Over the past few weeks, Singapore has become the talking point around the world.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, the reason for this undue attention really makes us feel very uneasy and helpless.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some people take this opportunity to utter all kinds of things, hoping that everything would become chaotic.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Even more Singaporeans feel most dismayed by this development, not wishing to see the image of our country and the dignity of our leaders tarnished as a result.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has transformed from a small fishing village into an independent and developed nation, becoming one of the most competitive cities globally.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This did not occur by chance, but derived from the far-sightedness of our Pioneer leaders, the citizens' unity and hard work, the Government's diligence and pragmatism, making all efforts to maintain social cohesion and promote economic development.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Presently, the world is not really at peace.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Many countries around the world are facing all kinds of problems, and Singapore is no exception.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the past, we have also encountered setbacks, but our people believed that an open and transparent political system and a government which is administratively robust, would enable everyone to overcome difficulties together.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: An ancient saying goes that an honest and upright official finds it hard to judge domestic affairs, as every household experiences its own specific problems.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I am not making any judgements, but I do love my country and respect our Pioneer leaders even more.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this constantly changing international order, Singapore's economic restructuring has entered a difficult period.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Coupled with domestic and external threats from extremist groups, we deeply believe that the Prime Minister and Ministers would continue to put national interests as their top priority.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I recall that two years ago, here in Parliament, I gave an eulogy at a tribute to Founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I said that "the most valuable legacy that Mr Lee Kuan Yew has left behind is the nation, system and political ideology that he forged together with his comrades".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We should endeavour to make it even better, enabling the task of nation-building that he had struggled to achieve in his lifetime to flourish.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Fifty years of nation-building have enabled fellow Singaporeans to enjoy the benefits of economic growth and stability in our society.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As we carry Singapore passports, we feel a great sense of pride for our country wherever we go.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, during this period, Singapore has become the target of sensational news.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We should not carry our Singapore passport in one hand and go around the world to open up our minds or seek business opportunities and enjoy the convenience and respect from every country, and yet, on the other hand, cast doubts and distrust on our country's political system.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Even more disastrous is that when other people cast aspersions on our own country, we choose to keep quiet or avoid replying, unwilling or not daring to come forward in defence.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This red passport is accepted worldwide because it symbolises the transparency and reliability of Singapore's political system.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If Singaporeans cannot respect ourselves, lose self-respect, lose trust in our own country's political system, how can we expect to earn respect from others?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some businessmen have complained to me that recently, whenever they meet business partners abroad, they are always being queried about this dispute and are nonplussed about the appropriate way to respond.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I think everyone should stand up and bravely defend the dignity of our nation and our leaders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Prime Minister, you had asked that all MPs be candid and ask any questions so as to allow you to clarify matters fully and put to rest any doubt what the allegations of abuse of your powers are and the aspersions cast on the integrity of the system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is with this spirit in mind that I seek clarification on a few matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a lawyer, I typically extol the advantages of having a will to my clients.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It helps your loved ones deal with your assets when you pass on and you can ensure that your wishes are carried out when you are not around.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I have also seen cases where things go awry and family members disagree on the validity of the will after the individual has passed away.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, important that a will is properly drafted and proper independent legal advice is given to the client to avoid any doubt or challenge to the will.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the circumstances, I find it unsettling that it is not clear who drafted the will.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is odd that we do not know this answer and there are issues as to whether the late Mr Lee was independently advised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Anyone who knows the law would know that you need someone independent to draft the will.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are serious assertions which may go towards the validity of the will and the propriety of Mdm Lee Suet Fern as a lawyer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The proper forum to challenge a will and raise these issues would be in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A fight in Court, especially between family members, can be emotionally draining and damaging to the relationship.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, while your reluctance to contest the grant of probate and your initial decision not to challenge the will is understandable, there are, therefore, now questions raised about the appropriateness to now raise these issues before the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: You had, however, in your statutory declaration submitted to the Ministerial Committee alluded to certain questionable circumstances upon which the will was executed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This may appear to be a "backdoor" approach in challenging the validity of the will.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Why could you not just rely on the words of the will which, in itself, contemplated a situation where the house is not being demolished?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Related to the above, many have raised concerns on the formation of the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Prime Minister, it is noted that you had recused yourself from making any decisions on 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, some are still not convinced that the Ministers are able to put aside their deference to you in relation to this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Personally, I am not quite sure what the Ministers need to defer to you on as there is no decision to be made at this juncture, given that Dr Lee Wei Ling is still staying at the house.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am also not clear of the benefits you gain whether the house is demolished or not.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there is now doubt on the improper use of your powers in setting up this Committee.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand and I note from Deputy Prime Minister Teo's earlier explanation that the Ministerial Committee came about as a result of a proposal put up by the Minister of National Development.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe it would help to dissipate any doubt if you could clarify on this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My next question relates to the Deed of Gift entered into by Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang with NHB.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As highlighted by Minister Lawrence Wong, there were some strange conditions in the Deed, which included the right of the executors to buy back the items for $1 and a display of a partial quote of the demolition clause in the late Mr Lee's will.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The much-quoted demolition clause has two parts; the first part expresses the late Mr and Mrs Lee's wish that the house at 38 Oxley Road be demolished.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The second part showed that Mr Lee had, in fact, contemplated the situation when the house could not be demolished.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Deed had only asked for only the first part of the will to be prominently displayed to the public.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Should you also not have a more rigorous process to check whether or not there was a consent of all the beneficiaries obtained?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Was there a proper process in place to vet the terms of the Deed and consider whether it was appropriate to enter into the Deed with the Lee siblings?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have also found it disturbing that Mdm Lee Suet Fern was involved in this decision, and may I just seek clarification on the rigour in the process in determining the suitability of entering into this Deed with the two of them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   The issue concerning 38 Oxley Road has caused unease among Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The integrity of the leadership and system of Government are being questioned.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There appears to be a slight loss of faith in the Government that was elected by the people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is very sad and will have serious implications on our country's international standing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I truly hope that all the questions raised can be answered fully so that there will be no more lingering doubts about the transparency and integrity of the Government.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And I also hope that after this debate, all of us can fully focus on the efforts to prepare our society for our future challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English) In the past few weeks, the integrity of the system and leadership has been called into question.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Upon listening to Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary's speech as well as some of my other colleagues, it reminded me that the closure on whether or not we achieve this is up to us Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As my Parliamentary colleague Dr Tan Wu Meng said, "If we have any questions, any queries, Internet is still open.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is up to us to just put up the questions and allow the Prime Minister to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It decides to convene an extraordinary general meeting (EOGM) of shareholders to debate the allegations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, at the EOGM, the CEO rebuts the Facebook posts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He then asks for a vote of shareholders to decide if he should step down.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No independent investigation of the claims made, just settled by debate after hearing one side of the story.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would such a company be deemed to have met best practices of corporate governance?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would such a company be seen to be beyond reproach?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the process we follow to resolve this issue that I will focus on in my speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall not speak on the issue of what should be done to the house at 38 Oxley Road or what the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew wanted for his house, questions on which the WP does not adopt a Party position, as my colleagues have explained.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If allowed to fester, these allegations will damage Singapore even more in the weeks and months ahead.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They must be decisively addressed, the truth established and appropriate follow-up actions taken in respect of the events and incidence themselves as well as any systemic issues that need to be attended to, to prevent a recurrence of similar incidences in future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever happens today and tomorrow in Parliament − whatever attacks are levelled against the accusers, whatever compromises are suggested, whatever admissions of error or wrongdoing are made − we cannot dismiss such allegations without allowing to the accusers a public platform to defend and expand on their views, share their evidence and be cross-examined, a public platform where all can see justice being done.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Otherwise the matter may never be put to bed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The conclusions made in this House in the wrapping-up speeches after this debate may simply be rebutted on Facebook the next day with reference to fresh information.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The erosion of public and international confidence may continue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, in his Facebook post of Thursday, 29 June, Mr Lee Hsien Yang stated, "We have begun to show evidence of his misuse of his position and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Note the choice of the word "begun." Can anyone seriously maintain that we can properly and finally put these allegations to rest once and for all simply by debating amongst ourselves in this House today?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nor should we settle for a debate today that ends on the question: do you have confidence in the Government or not, are you calling for the resignation of key figures or not?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is my view that this should not be the way to deal with these allegations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a time for calls of "are you for me or against me." To those who might think to make such a call today or tomorrow, I ask you: why are you afraid of a proper, public fact-finding process that allows the accusers to testify and be cross-examined?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will now speak about some issues related to the allegations of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo said that the Ministerial Committee on 38 Oxley Road was convened to explore options.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is an established process for gazetting a building as a national monument or some equivalent of that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why were the established channels not used in this case?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe other MPs have spoken about this as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, it might be argued that perhaps this case is not like others, because deference needs to be shown to the wishes of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if that is the stance of the Government, why was a non-transparent Ministerial Committee chosen as the right organisational form for resolving this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not some kind of independent panel with the expertise and resources to perform expert heritage analysis and public opinion sensing?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A panel that would not be seen by anyone as potentially compromised by the fact that its members directly report to an individual who has personal ties to the matter at hand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even more importantly, the Ministerial Committee seems to have focused primarily on revisiting the issue of the wishes of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew as expressed in his last will.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe several Members have spoken about this already.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Cabinet Secretary made a statement on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister released portions of his statutory declaration relating to this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State for Law Ms Indranee Rajah released several Facebook posts on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, the proper platform to challenge the late Mr Lee's will would have been in Court.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, other than revisiting the issue of what the late Mr Lee wanted, there would appear to be little evidence available to date of any other work done by the Ministerial Committee in respect of work streams, such as heritage impact assessment, public opinion sensing and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why did the Ministerial Committee and other PAP politicians focus so much on the issue of what the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew wanted?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why was the machinery of Government applied to take up a position on a private family matter of a will which had never been litigated in Court?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is opening questions about the late Mr Lee's will without going to the Courts the legitimate business for the Government of Singapore as opposed to being merely a legitimate concern for one individual member of that Government in his individual capacity?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, the process of independent fact-finding favoured by members of the PAP was suing for defamation in Court and that is certainly one way to resolve this matter definitively.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The follow-up action could relate to the incidents at hand and it could also relate to systemic changes the Committee may propose to curtail the ability of future officeholders to abuse their powers or to clarify any grey areas in the current rules that may have enabled this unfortunate series of events to occur, to prevent their recurrence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Committee's independence would be underscored by the presence of non-PAP MPs on the Committee.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, in his message on 19 June, the Prime Minister specifically highlighted that non-PAP MPs would be able to question him in Parliament today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Parliamentary Select Committee merely builds on that institutional recipe of multi-partisanship that the Prime Minister himself positively alluded to but extends it to include a process of fact-finding involving public hearings and cross-examination of the individuals who have laid these issues before the nation, together with other persons of interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the claims are baseless, the accusers will lose credibility in a very public way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there is a basis to their claims, that can be acknowledged and followed up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would note on this point that several Members of the House today have posed questions quite literally to Mr Lee Hsien Yang.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we envisage Mr Lee Hsien Yang is meant to properly and in an institutional form respond to these questions that have been posed and asked today and he is not here to respond to them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore is strengthened, not weakened when we not only do the right thing but we are seen to be doing the right thing by giving the accusers a right to make their case, be cross-examined and rebut replies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the dinner table two days ago, when we discussed this issue in my family, my daughter asked me, "Daddy, why are they ensnaring us in their family quarrel?" My answer to her was, "I'm not sure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo has said that he personally would not support options at either end of the range.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the one end, preserving the house for visitors to enter and see, which would be totally against the wishes of Mr and Mrs Lee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the other hand, demolishing the house and putting the property on the market for new private residences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Initially, Mr Lee Hsien Yang said, he had "not thought beyond demolition".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If that is true, he could not have ruled out redevelopment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then, he later said that before the Ministerial Committee was formed, he had offered a memorial garden.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, it appears that he had thought beyond demolition, earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He did not make it clear if a garden is still his position now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: After I pointed out the four possible options for the property, including the fact that demolition clears the way to appeal for redevelopment, Mr Lee Hsien Yang now says that he has no "inclination" to develop the house for profit. "Inclination" is a word that leaves a lot of room for change of mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If he changes his mind, then the land is potentially worth a lot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Why does Mr Lee Hsien Yang not just rule it out categorically?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But let us take his statement at face value and see what else Mr Lee Hsien Yang said on Saturday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: His exact words were "preservation of the house would be trampling on Mr Lee Kuan Yew's values, and it would be an affront to these same values to develop a luxury "LKY" condominium".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Well, is not that exactly the same thing that Deputy Prime Minister Teo had said, leaving aside the bit about values?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In other words, no total preservation and no development?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If that is the case and if he is saying exactly the same thing as Deputy Prime Minister Teo, where is the dispute?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Both agree that the extreme ends of the range are out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, if the Ministerial Committee is studying the intermediate options within the range, what is wrong with that?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: How can studying these options be an abuse?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the will, the concerns of Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee with the Ministerial Committee and all the allegations appear to have been triggered by questions on the will.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We know from the facts disclosed that issues have been raised with regard to the will and who drafted it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If it was drafted by Mrs Lee Suet Fern, then an issue arises because she is the wife of Mr Lee Hsien Yang and his share of the estate was increased under the last will.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As our Court of Appeal has said, "the preparation of a will involves serious professional responsibilities which solicitors must uncompromisingly observe and discharge".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, if the lawyer has an interest in the will, the lawyer must make sure that the person making the will gets independent advice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some have said, "But Mr Lee was a very good lawyer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Are you saying he did not know what he was signing?" No one is saying that at all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The issue is whether he received independent advice as the law uncompromisingly requires.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And we do know that Mr Lee had consistently in his lifetime taken independent advice − for his lawsuits and for his first six wills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo has already explained that the Ministerial Committee looked at the will as part of trying to understand Mr Lee's thinking on the matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The terms of the will, insofar as they relate to the house, would be relevant to that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The siblings provided different views on the drafting of the will.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Each party was given the opportunity to comment on the other side's views, as is only fair.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is simply trying to understand, as best it can, what were Mr Lee's wishes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, really, there is no basis for all these allegations that have been levelled against the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat read out a catalogue of allegations from the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Is he associating himself with these allegations, or simply regurgitating them?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If he is adopting them, then please put forward some specific evidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Png also referred to allegations that improper influence had been asserted over civil servants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is a very serious allegation, not only against Ms Ho Ching, but also against the Permanent Secretaries and senior civil servants as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are clear rules within the Civil Service to guide the conduct of public officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Png referred to the cataloguing of Mr Lee's items.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The involvement of MCI photographers is in line with MCI's policy of supporting former Prime Ministers and Presidents after they leave office.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: After Mr Lee's passing, MCI photographers were deployed to take photos of various personal and official items belonging to Mr Lee at 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was done for the purposes of national archival and documentation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similar photographic recordings were done during Mr Lee's lifetime, of his study at home, and of the basement dining room.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If there are any specific instances of alleged impropriety beyond that, these should be identified, rather than making general unsubstantiated allegations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are stringent rules in place and serious consequences for those who have been found to have contravened the rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Questions about alleged conflict on the part of the Attorney-General (AG) were asked.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The laws and rules on conflict are very clear.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They have abided by the rules of conflict, and there is no basis to suggest that either the AG or the Deputy AG has not observed those rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: An example of how the rules work would be when lawyers move from AG's Chambers (AGC) to the Bench and vice versa.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, take, for example, former Deputy AG Tan Siong Thye, who was from AGC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He recuses himself from any AGC-related matters, now that he has returned to the Bench.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Likewise, the Chief Justice, in relation to any matters he handled when he was at AGC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similar rules apply in private practice as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If a lawyer moves to a new firm, he observes the rules on conflict.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He does not involve himself in his new firm on matters which his old firm had acted for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This has been debated before, in relation to the appointment of the AG and Deputy AG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Lucien Wong, we have already referred to his credentials previously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He was the senior partner of the largest law firm in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He is widely acknowledged as the top legal mind, consistently recognised as one of Singapore's best, and his appointment was welcomed by the Bar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Law Society has called him "a formidable and creative legal mind" with "proven management skills", a "practical track record" and a "skillset uniquely equipped to deal with the evolution of the changing legal environment in Singapore".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a lawyer of almost 40 years' standing, Mr Wong would have had thousands of clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is no reason why this should be an excuse for us to pass him over and choose a less qualified candidate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Similarly, Mr Hri Kumar is amongst one of the top six to seven litigators in Singapore today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If you look at the people from within the Service who have been appointed to key positions − the Deputy AG and the Solicitor-General as well − these are young, some of them in their 40s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We hope that, in the future, from among their ranks, someone can become AG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Prime Minister consulted the Chief Justice and the Chairman of Public Service Commission and the incumbent AG on the appointment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is also not unusual for the AG to be known to the Ministers or the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members will recall that the Law Minister, Mr Edmund Barker, was very successful, one of our founding fathers, and was an old friend of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, and a partner in Lee & Lee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This did not prevent him from being a good Law Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With respect to past judicial appointments, these have included lawyers who acted for Mr Lee Kuan Yew, such as Mr Joseph Grimberg, or who worked in Lee & Lee, for example, Justice Lai Kew Chai, and Mr Andrew Ang, who is currently on the Bench.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All were or are well-respected members of the Bench.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Former Chief Justice Yong Pung How was an old friend of Mr Lee's from Cambridge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He is credited with modernising the Singapore Judiciary during his time on the Bench.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In these roles, all of them observed the appropriate conflict rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ultimately, the most important considerations are the quality, character and the integrity of the individuals involved, and that is the hallmark of our system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And, indeed, in many first-world countries, the AG is even a sitting member of parliament or a politician.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the United Kingdom, the AG is a Cabinet minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our system is based on a slightly different model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But as I have said before, it goes too far to suggest that AGC officers must not have previously had any links with any Ministers or political party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the questions about alleged conflict regarding Minister Shanmugam, Mr Low Thia Khiang's comment on him being Mr Lee's friend − well, being a friend of Mr Lee Kuan Yew does not disqualify him from doing Cabinet work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes being in the Ministerial Committee to give views.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Low alluded to Dr Lee Wei Ling's comment that Minister Shanmugam was a "changed person".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Well, she has said many things about many people, including the Prime Minister, members of Cabinet and others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singaporeans will look at the facts and reach their own conclusions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the issue of whether Minister Shanmugam is somehow in a position of "conflict", he has explained his position publicly on 17 June.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2011, some members of the Lee family had approached him for his views about various options for the house.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He shared some thoughts and suggestions with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, he also made clear to them that legally, the Government had the full power to gazette or acquire based on historical significance, and that many Singaporeans, including Ministers in Cabinet, were likely to take the view that the house should be preserved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He told them that this was also his strong personal view.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew had spoken with other Cabinet Ministers about the house as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It would be absurd to suggest that they can all no longer participate in Government work because they had spoken to him, or some family member about the house.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is really a red herring, intended to divert attention away from the real issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And so, we come back to the key point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Indeed, nothing can be decided now as Dr Lee is still living in the house.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Therefore, the house cannot be the reason for the dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The trigger for all the allegations by Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee appear to be something else.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Whatever it is, there is no reason to drag Singapore and Singaporeans through this dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is contrary to Mr Lee Kuan Yew's values.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leon Perera gave the analogy of a company and its shareholders and he asked why the whistleblowers are not being interrogated by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If something is really wrong, then the correct thing for the whistleblowers to do is to go to CPIB and file a report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is the way it should be done if you think that there is something wrong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Or if anyone else thinks that something is wrong, you can file and lodge a formal report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the Ministerial Committee, Mr Leon Perera may wish to look again at the Deputy Prime Minister's speech today where he explained the role and the terms of reference of the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, what do we have at the end of the day?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the end of today, we have had one full day of debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Parliament, no one has said that there is any evidence of abuse.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I am sure that the MPs have all looked carefully through the allegations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, Mr Low himself had said that the siblings had presented no evidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To me, that is most significant because it shows our people that these allegations are just that − allegations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, she told the House that the AG and the Deputy AG have been observing the conflict rules in their functions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification is that the Senior Minister of State mentioned the fact that there have been friends of Ministers who have been appointed to various Organs of State – and I think she mentioned the Judiciary is one of them – does she not agree that for the AGC, what we are faced with now is not the Judiciary where there is security of tenure, where Judges are appointed and secured until age 65, but we have an AG now who is on a short-term contract of three years?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That puts a very different complexion on things.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The third clarification is: does the Senior Minister of State agree or not agree that it is desirable to have distance between the AGC leadership and the Government, which was what was believed by some former Ministers, including Prof Jayakumar, or have standards changed?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the very simple reason that in AGC, there are other officers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you had acted on something, and you happen to change organisation or go somewhere else, and there is a conflict, you recuse yourself.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not a difficult thing to do, and lawyers do it in practice all the time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The AG and Deputy AG are observing these rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I can assure Ms Sylvia Lim that the rules of conflict are being observed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the other point, Ms Sylvia Lim said it is different from the Bench where there is security of tenure but in AGC there is no security of tenure which puts a different complexion on things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not put a different complexion on things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All lawyers, good lawyers, understand their duty, which is simply this: if you are in a position of conflict, you do not act, you recuse yourself.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As to whether it is desirable to have distance, the correct question really is, the officers of AGC, do they act independently?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, if there is a conflict, do they stand aside?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Do they apply their minds to this without fear or favour?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the answer to those questions is yes, they do act independently, they apply their minds and they carry out their duties without fear or favour.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in short, the officers in the AGC, whether it is the AG, Deputy AG or anyone down along the line, all observe proper rules of conduct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Is she saying that the Deputy AG, because he may not have acted on the Lee estate in some capacity in private estate, is now free to advise the Government on such matters, from the Government's perspective?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification is that the Senior Minister of State did not answer directly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: She said I asked the wrong question about whether there should be distance between the AGC and the Government because the critical question to her was the officers act professionally and independently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But this is really quite a different take for even Prof Jayakumar.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: If you read what his interview goes into, he says that he may occasionally have working lunches with the AG but it is important to have the appearance of distance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: You cannot get too close to these people because people might assume that there will be some compromise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I think it is the appearance itself that is important, not just, in fact, whether people think they are able to act independently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The appearance when you are too close to somebody, it does not create a good feeling.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the other matters, I have already explained.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There have been instances before when either the AG or Judges may have been close friends with Ministers or anyone else, but that has not deterred them from doing their duty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: She is saying actual conflict and, sort of, appearances.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In terms of any actual conflict, I have already stated the position quite clearly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They know their duty and they will carry out their duty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will not act where there is any conflict of interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as far as appearances go, if the Member has any specific allegation of that, please highlight it.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, please confine your clarifications to matters which Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah has said.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Deputy Speaker, first of all, the Senior Minister of State seems to suggest that I said there is no evidence.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But the question then is, how would the member of public or anyone else know, whether in such a particular case, I mean, the AG stands aside or does he not stand aside?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Thereby, my question is: important appointments like such, even the Minister for Law or senior judges and so on, the public perception of its independence and impartiality is important.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Is it not important or is it important?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Next, if there is a question of doubt, then what should the Government do?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Next, a point of clarification actually on a point of order that I wish to clarify with the Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I heard the Senior Minister of State's speech earlier on.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: She seems to be attacking Lee Hsien Yang and imputing some character or motive.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: He is not here in the House to answer.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State, do you want to respond to the point of order?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: That Mr Low has said that you were saying something against Mr Lee Hsien Yang.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All I did was point out that there were certain allegations made against the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And there is nothing at all that prevents Mr Lee Hsien Yang from responding if he wishes to, publicly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All I am doing is stating the Government's position on various issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On conflicts of interest, I have already answered that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not necessary for me to repeat it again.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I had initially hoped that the dispute is just a family dispute which many other families would have.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Unfortunately, the allegations made by the two younger siblings of the Prime Minister go beyond a dispute whether to demolish 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The two of them allege that the Prime Minister had misused his position and influence over the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They further allege that the system has no checks or balance to prevent abuse of Government and fear the use of Organs of State against the two of them and Suet Fern.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Are they saying that our Deputy Prime Minister, the Ministers and other officebearers are subservient to the Prime Minister's wishes and cannot think for themselves?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That the senior civil servants would set aside their personal beliefs and convictions just to obey the Prime Minister blindly without question?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The allegations of abuse are short on details and not substantiated.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After reading several of the media releases of Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling, I surmised that the crux of the siblings' unhappiness is that the Prime Minister failed to comply with the desire of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew to demolish 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They are unhappy that a Ministerial Committee was set up to consider the options regarding 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, because these allegations of abuse came from no less a person than the Prime Minister's own siblings and they attack the integrity of the leader of the Government, it behoves the Prime Minister and other Cabinet Ministers involved to set out the basis for their decisions so that they can be scrutinised by members of the public.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is Parliament the proper place to discuss these issues?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have no doubt because the allegations go towards the question of whether there was abuse of power and this affects the integrity of the Government and the system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the Prime Minister does not defend the allegations in Parliament, where does he do so?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Prime Minister has also invited all Members of Parliament to speak freely and ask queries so that he can clear any doubts which we, Members of Parliament, as representatives of the people may have.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And we have seen PAP Members of Parliament, Opposition Members of Parliament and Nominated Members of Parliament rise to ask many questions yesterday.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the Members of Parliament who had called on Prime Minister Lee to sue, I felt a sense of dismay.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How many of us present in Parliament today would truly want to sue our own siblings or even relatives in Court for defamation?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Whatever unhappiness that we may have with our own siblings, our own brother or sister, would we really, really want to take them to Court?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would you not think of how your parents would feel if they see their own children squabbling so publicly or, worse, sue each other in Court?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of us, each time we read in the newspaper about a child suing their parents or a sibling suing another sibling, we shake our heads in dismay.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Prime Minister said yesterday right at the start of his speech that he was not in Parliament to make a case against his siblings.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But what is private, he will try to resolve privately.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For that statement, he has my utmost respect.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are certain queries which the public has and I hope that the Prime Minister's answers will clear the air.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of the queries have already been answered in the Ministerial Statements yesterday.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Were there any decisions made by Ministers within the Committee because the Prime Minister had explicitly directed them?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How much influence did the Prime Minister have in the decision whether to demolish or not to demolish 38 Oxley Road?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Did the Committee consult the Prime Minister before any decision was made even though he had recused himself from any decision on the property?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How can members of the public be assured that Cabinet members involved in the decision would make rational decisions and not worry that they would lose their jobs if they were to make a wrong decision about Oxley Road?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Were they in awe of the Prime Minister and would defer to his wishes even though those wishes were not expressed?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think these questions are best answered by Deputy Prime Minister Teo, as any reply by the Prime Minister may be seen to be self-serving.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Could Mr Lee Hsien Yang be frustrated with the fact that after buying the property at full market value, he now finds out that the Government is unwilling to allow the demolition of the property or is not ready to allow any re-development of the property?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Was Mr Lee Hsien Yang aware that the Government is still deliberating about what to do with Oxley Road when the Prime Minister offered to sell the property to him at full value?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Prime Minister and the Government to share as much information as possible so that the citizens of Singapore can continue to have confidence in the political system and the rule of governance within the Singapore Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, I refer to the statement by Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling regarding the desire by Minister Mentor Lee Kuan Yew to demolish 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The allegation about the Prime Minister's abuse of power seems to centre on their unhappiness that a Ministerial Committee was set up to consider the options about the future of 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Had this property been any apartment or condominium, I would have agreed that this is a private matter.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But, unfortunately, the property concerned is 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many Singaporeans recognise that 38 Oxley Road holds special historical significance to Singapore and the late Minister Mentor Lee would have recognised this fact as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year, I filed an Adjournment Motion and appealed to the Government to consider the preservation of the Dakota Crescent rental flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At that time, I lamented at "the demolition and loss of other prominent buildings like the National Library, the National Theatre, the Van Kleef Aquarium and Queensway Cinema".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I argued that our children and the future generations should not be left to read about Singapore's heritage, culture and history only through history textbooks, photographs or some sanitised heritage trails." Because 38 Oxley Road holds greater historical significance and heritage value to Singaporeans, I agree that we ought to consider all options for this property because, once demolished, part of our history would be gone forever, permanently.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, whilst many of us understand the reason why Minister Mentor Lee wanted to demolish 38 Oxley Road, I would be greatly disappointed if the Prime Minister had ordered the Government to demolish the Oxley Road property without going through due process of considering the heritage and historical value of the property.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the Prime Minister had done so, this means that Minister Mentor Lee's wishes are above the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How then will the Government account to Singaporeans whose properties were previously conserved against their wishes?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If 38 Oxley Road had been demolished without due process to consider the value of conserving the property, many Singaporeans would then have accused the Prime Minister of having a different law for Mr Lee Kuan Yew as compared to other Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This would truly be an abuse of his position as Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, I cannot understand why Mr Lee Hsien Yang would claim that the Prime Minister had abused his position.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Prime Minister Lee had a duty to all Singaporeans to consider the heritage value of 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even as the experts review the options for 38 Oxley Road, I urge the Government to ascertain what were the exact wishes of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew regarding 38 Oxley Road, a property of historical significance.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling had claimed in their media release that the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew removed the Prime Minister as executor and had specifically inserted into his will his wish for 38 Oxley Road to be demolished.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have two concerns after I read the statutory declaration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: First, why did the Prime Minister not challenge the will if he had doubts about the circumstances behind the making of the will?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why did he allow the Grant of Probate to be extracted without challenge?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, the lawyer shall advise the client to seek independent advice in respect of the gift.
