speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Singapore Court of Appeal had also stated that a solicitor, before preparing a will, should discuss the matter with the testator on the legal issues.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is a basic fundamental principle that most lawyers would be aware of.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The rationale for the rule is really to avoid any potential conflict of interest, to avoid any allegation that there was undue pressure on the testator by the witness and to ensure that the testator has been independently advised.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang, in his Facebook post, had said that Ms Kwa Kim Li from Lee & Lee had drafted the will.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why did Mr Lee Hsien Yang say this?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Subsequently, he said in a Facebook posting that his wife, Ms Lee Suet Fern, had put the will into language.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is this a roundabout way of saying that the will was drafted by his wife?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: She then asked her firm's lawyers to witness Minister Mentor Lee's execution of the will.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If there had been any misconduct in relation to the drafting of the will, then it is no longer a private matter.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope the matter will be treated with proper seriousness by the authorities.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: No one should be above the law, regardless of whether the person is the Prime Minister himself, Mr Lee Kuan Yew's children or anyone related to the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The challenge by Mr Lee Hsien Yang is that Prime Minister Lee is abusing his authority to ask Cabinet to preserve 38 Oxley Road against the wishes of Minister Mentor Lee.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that the Government has an obligation to better understand what Minister Mentor Lee's wishes were.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It raises both serious legal and moral questions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For many Singaporeans, the quarrel is not just about the Oxley Road property.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are ways of resolving this dispute without the need to make such public accusations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even if Prime Minister Lee does agree with his father's desire to demolish the property, I would say that Prime Minister Lee still owes a duty to Singaporeans to consider the preservation of the property.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What grieves me and many of my residents is that these allegations have brought dishonour to the name of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our first Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The continuation of these baseless accusations distract the Government from its actual duty of providing leadership for the country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But sadly, from this morning's response, it seems that this is unlikely.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The legacy of Minister Mentor Lee seems likely to be damaged by the continued accusations and I would say Singaporeans just have to move on.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: This is particularly so as it is not clear whether there are any actionable steps which can be taken with the survey results.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: (b) what will the data in the poll be used for?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: The statements and postings made by both sides of this dispute have exposed a deep rift within the Lee family.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Whether people care to admit it or not, Mr Lee Kuan Yew and the Lee family name are inextricably linked with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: For many Singaporeans, conflict of this nature within the Lee family extends beyond being just a private family dispute, especially when so many public allegations and counter allegations have been made and continue to be made, particularly on the way we govern ourselves.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: And then, there are the other related issues as to the way we behave towards each other and the example we set for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: There is a sense of disquiet because, for those of us who consider Mr Lee Kuan Yew as the foremost founding father of modern Singapore and the legacy that he has left us, we feel personally affected.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: We feel that Mr Lee Kuan Yew would not wish to see his family in this current state.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: But more importantly, I think Mr Lee Kuan Yew would not wish to see his family affairs demolish the standing and the reputation of Singapore that he had spent his lifetime building.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I do not think anyone would dispute that this is what Mr Lee Kuan Yew would want for his family and for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: And I think this is also what most Singaporeans hope would happen because there are no real winners in this sad episode.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure those beneficiaries will be very grateful for the substantial donations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   In the Prime Minister's Statement on 19 June, he urged Members of Parliament to raise all questions without reservation with him and the relevant Ministers on the serious allegations raised by his siblings, in order to clear any doubts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, abuse of power is a very serious allegation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It violates the core governing principles and values which Singapore has been upholding all along.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These accusations will affect public confidence and trust in the Government and the system of governance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have, indeed, responded to the Prime Minister's appeal and had wanted to raise some tough questions with the Prime Minister and the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, after seven hours of debate yesterday, including the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister's detailed Statements with attached documents, several Ministers and more than 20 Members' speeches, what should be asked has been asked and we have heard reasonable answers to almost all of them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I cannot find any other allegation that warrants further questioning.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, if the Prime Minister did not follow normal procedures and gave instructions to the Cabinet and relevant agencies to demolish the house in order to fulfil his late father's wishes, that would actually be a case of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I cannot see anything improper with setting up the Ministerial Committee led by Deputy Prime Minister Teo to look at the various options for the house and the Prime Minister recusing himself from it.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not see any evidence of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, this is the normal workings of the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yesterday, the Prime Minister and Minister Lawrence Wong addressed the issue of the Deed of Gift, explaining under what circumstance the Prime Minster got hold of the Deed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Looking at the entire process of NHB's dealings with the Estate Executors on the exhibition of items from the house, we have discovered some other areas that are not quite right.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, one of the beneficiaries, that is, the Prime Minister, was totally unaware of the Deed of Gift and the Deed of Gift contains certain unusual clauses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More seriously, the role that Ms Lim Suet Fern played in the process gave rise to suspicion of conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am not going to repeat the questions that other hon Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling's 14 June post, they claimed that Mr Lee Kuan Yew, after coming back from the meeting with the Cabinet, was anguished and despondent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, I would like to reflect my residents' views on this dispute and their expectations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As this is a matter of a family dispute going public, many Singaporeans have felt upset and sad.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because Singaporeans never expected that this could happen to Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our beloved founding Prime Minister who Singaporeans are grateful to.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans are also concerned because this incident happened to our Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Prime Minister is not only the eldest son of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, he is also the top leader of our Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This incident would definitely cause some degree of damage to our reputation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Prime Minister had stated before that he had always wanted to settle his disagreement with his siblings within the family.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, now, since the dispute has been made public, the Government has no choice but to respond in order to restore the confidence of the people in the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And the Prime Minister has also apologised to the people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Every family has its own difficulties and, within the family, it is common that different members have different views on certain issues.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans do not wish to be part of this family dispute.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Looking at the exchanges on Facebook, people feel upset and helpless.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A resident told me that he had stopped reading or following the postings and allegations on social media.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many people cannot bear to see this kind of dispute happening to the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew and the family of Prime Minister Lee.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They do not wish to choose sides in this family dispute.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They feel that they have somehow been dragged into this dispute inadvertently.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think many Singaporeans hope that this dispute will come to an end quickly and be resolved within the family so that the Government and society can focus its energy on more serious issues and challenges that are facing us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure Singaporeans would like to know what is next after today's debate in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can we get out of this cycle of allegations?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we deal with the impact of this dispute thereafter?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, this is not a problem that we need to address immediately.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The political situation in the world is changing rapidly and has brought about much uncertainty for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tomorrow, Prime Minister Lee will be going to Hamburg to attend the G20 meeting.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although Singapore is not a member of the G20, Singapore has been invited by the host country every year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This time, the Prime Minister will be meeting President Trump for the first time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We hope that the Prime Minister will make good progress in his discussions with various Heads of State during this trip and continue to widen the economic development space for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coming back to today's topic, of course, as Singaporeans, we should be concerned about allegations of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, we must also have confidence in the system which we have built up over the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although our system is not perfect, many countries envy us and want to learn from us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although we are a small island without any natural resources, we have been able to continuously adapt to the external environment, grow, create economic miracles and raise the standard of living for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not something that can be achieved by a Government that has abused its power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this time, we need a strong, capable and decisive Government in order to meet the various short- and long-term challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The trust and confidence of the people in Government leaders are absolutely important and are key to our success.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We cannot turn back the clock to go back to before 14 June.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The accusations have brought invisible harm but there is no use crying over spilt milk.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we should do now is to rebuild confidence and trust in our system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Prime Minister and the eldest son of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, the Prime Minister is in a dilemma between the country and the family on how to deal with 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may well be the root cause of the dispute between him and his siblings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We look forward to the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister's replies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I served as Mr Lee Kuan Yew's Principal Private Secretary, or PPS, when he was Senior Minister, from mid-1997 to early 2000.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During that period, I had the benefit of many interactions with Mr Lee.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I also interacted with Mrs Lee, both in Singapore and on several overseas trips.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I learnt that both of them, especially Mrs Lee, valued their privacy deeply.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They would be deeply anguished if they were alive to see the siblings' disagreement played out so publicly.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Teo have addressed these allegations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members have also given their views on this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I hope Members of this House and other Singaporeans will reflect on these and decide for themselves if any abuse has taken place.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What has been levelled are general allegations and aspersions cast.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The two days of this Parliament sitting bear this out.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: No Member, including from the Workers' Party, has articulated any specific allegation of abuse of power.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I would, therefore, not dwell on the issues that have already been discussed quite extensively.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It has been only a little over two years since Mr Lee passed away.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The memory of the outpouring of grief at that time is still fresh in the hearts and minds of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We committed ourselves then to honour the ideals and principles of Mr Lee and our founding leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today, we should revisit this question calmly − what would Mr Lee's wish be?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I was PPS, Mr Lee was in the midst of writing his memoirs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He was almost 75 years old, and Mr Goh Chok Tong had been Prime Minister for seven years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Despite his age, Mr Lee worked with an amazing intensity.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over and above his daily work, he would labour deep into the early hours of the morning, every day, on the memoirs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During that time, Mr Lee met with many local and foreign visitors.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: From time to time, the visitors would ask Mr Lee what he was most concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over and over again, I heard Mr Lee say that he feared that the younger generation of Singaporeans might not understand what got us here and what we would need to do to continue to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: That was why he was labouring hard to distil the lessons of Singapore's development and share these with young Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, if you ask me what were the defining wishes of Mr Lee's life, I would say, Mr Lee's greatest wish was for Singapore to remain successful beyond his lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He dedicated his entire life to making a success of Singapore, against the odds.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The best way to honour him and to fulfil our duty to future generations of Singaporeans is to continue to work for the survival and success of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee said that there is no simple formula for running a country, but he tried to distil and pass on as many insights as he could.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can spend many hours debating the principles for Singapore's success.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee said that there was no textbook for running a country and that his memoirs were not a "how to" manual.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At different times, we would face different conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But he was convinced that we all need a sense of history − not just in knowing what happened in the past, but why it happened − that would help to anchor and guide us for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In 1980, at the 25th anniversary of the founding of the PAP, Mr Lee said: "To understand the present and anticipate the future, we must know enough of the past, enough to have a sense of the history of a people.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: One must appreciate not merely what took place but especially why it took place and in that particular way.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: That is true of individuals, as it is for nations." With that in mind, 38 Oxley Road holds special historical significance because of all the things that took place there in our early history.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In his memoirs, Mr Lee had a chapter on "Widening the Oxley Road circle", recounting how the founding fathers gathered in the basement dining room of Mr Lee's house, the birth of the People's Action Party in 1954, the difficult decisions they had to take whether to contest the elections in 1955 and 1959.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee also recounted how, during that tumultuous period, the Chinese school students "started turning up at Oxley Road looking for advice on a hundred and one problems they encountered whenever they came into conflict with or were obstructed by authority".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What happened in the basement dining room and at Oxley Road is relevant not just for the history of the PAP.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was surprised to hear Mr Png Eng Huat yesterday take such a narrow and partisan view of history.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Those years marked a pivotal moment in our nation's history − in fact, they were the start of a series of events that led to Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is, therefore, right and proper that we consider this history in any decision to demolish or preserve the house, or parts of it.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee stated his preference for the house to be demolished after his passing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Despite his seniority and his role as the founding Prime Minister of Singapore, he did not once use his status to advance his case.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He just stated his preference and then listened intently to the views of Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All of us who spoke felt deeply that, as a young nation, we needed a deeper sense of history and that the house was of historical significance.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked earlier if any Cabinet member had put any pressure on Mr Lee.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee looked very thoughtful after the session.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We did not hear from him until later, when he sent the note in December 2011 that the Prime Minister presented yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To me, that note, sent five months after the meeting, showed that he had been mulling over the issue during that period, and, importantly, he had taken other views on board.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Yesterday, Ms Chia Yong Yong spoke on the rule of law and what it meant to Mr Lee.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: She said, "I cannot imagine Mr Lee banging tables and insisting on the demolition of his house… I cannot imagine Mr Lee insisting that his individual interest must prevail over communitarian interest… I cannot imagine Mr Lee insisting that the Government cannot acquire his own property." She has put it very well.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee knew more than almost anyone the laws relating to the acquisition and preservation of property, having exercised powers over his years in office.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was at that Cabinet meeting and can attest that Mr Lee put his views to us, and then listened seriously to Cabinet members.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was struck at that time by how scrupulously he presented his case, without once invoking his seniority or contributions and how he listened so intently to what we had to say.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee's willingness to take into account new evidence and alternative views on the issue reminded me of how he had changed his view on language education for the young.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Bilingual education was Mr Lee's lifelong challenge and he studied the matter deeply.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I was PPS, there were those who advocated that children acquire languages better if they were exposed to them earlier, in their pre-school years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But, based on his own readings and experiences, he believed that the benefits of early exposure washed out as the child grows.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: More than a decade later, when I was Education Minister, Mr Lee asked to see me.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He told me that, after evaluating the evidence over the years, he was now convinced that there were benefits in giving young children early exposure to languages.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He asked that I guide MOE to use the fund to boost bilingualism across all levels, with special attention to the pre-school years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I share this experience to show Mr Lee's willingness to change his views if he was presented with robust arguments.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: His note to Cabinet on 38 Oxley Road, five months after he saw us, was an important change.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Cabinet had stated our case to Mr Lee and we did not expect to hear back from him.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Each time he had written on this issue to Cabinet had all been of his own volition, not at Cabinet's request.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, when he wrote to us in December 2011, it showed me two things: one, that he had taken five months to mull over very carefully; and, two, he felt that it was proper and important to inform Government of his thinking, now that he was prepared to consider the possibility that the Government of the day might decide not to demolish the house.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Until the Prime Minister shared it yesterday, I did not know that Mr Lee then went on to apply for URA approval to reinforce the foundations and renovate the house.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I do not want to venture into how Mr Lee's views might have changed further if he were alive today.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we must remember that Mr Lee's lifelong and unwavering dedication was to making a success of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: His efforts in his later years were about the success of Singapore beyond his lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I talked about Mr Lee's belief that we need a sense of history to keep Singapore successful.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The second principle for Singapore's success, which I would like to highlight and is relevant in this debate, is the rule of law.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: From what I have shared about that Cabinet meeting where Mr Lee came to give his views, and about his letter to Cabinet five months later, you would see that he observed a strict separation between his and Mrs Lee's private wish and the duty of Government.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He had a strong personality and formidable track record, but not once, not once, did he insist that only his view should prevail − exactly like Ms Chia Yong Yong had said.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I found that deeply admirable, for someone who was the founding Prime Minister of Singapore and who had been the Prime Minister for over 31 years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this regard, Members have heard the speeches of both the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Teo on how the Prime Minister recused himself from deliberations relating to the house and kept a strict separation between his private duty as a son, and his duty as the Head of Government.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As several Members have pointed out, the irony is that if the Prime Minister were to do what Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling wanted, to impose his private wishes as a son and have the house demolished, we would not have this disagreement made public, but he would have abused his power.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The third insight which I would like to share that Mr Lee had for Singapore's success was to keep Government honest and effective.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee devoted enormous amounts of effort to build up the Public Service, in persuading suitable men and women to stand as Members of Parliament and to testing some out as officeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He always put an emphasis on having a deep sense of values and service.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee believed profoundly in doing the right things, the necessary things.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this vein, both his sons took up SAF scholarships and both returned to serve in different ways.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The young Lee Hsien Loong was a Senior Wrangler at Cambridge University − the top Mathematics student in his year.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He could have devoted his life to Mathematics and probably have great success.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But he wrote to his tutor: "It is absolutely necessary that I remain in Singapore, whatever I do… because Singapore is where I belong and where I want to be." In fact, the young Lee Hsien Loong never told his parents about this; he simply came home and got to work in the SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew only learnt about it later.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is this deep sense of service for a young man in his early 20s.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members have cautioned that we must keep the Government's focus on the major issues confronting Singapore and not be distracted.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we have learnt in this debate, the family disagreement has been playing out over the last two years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Instead of allowing this episode to distract him or the Government, the Prime Minister has continued to focus, not just on the issues of the day, but on further laying the ground to address the medium and longer term challenges to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These relate to our security, foreign relations, jobs and the economy, healthcare and infrastructure, among others.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr and Mrs Lee's three children have each made their contribution to Singapore, in different ways.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Prime Minister has been in public service all his life and is still in public service.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang served in the SAF and later Singtel.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Dr Lee Wei Ling has been a passionate paediatric neurologist and built up the National Neuroscience Institute well when she was heading it.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I appreciate Dr Lee's care and concern for me when I was hospitalised last year.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: She remains Senior Advisor at the NNI and made the effort to visit and advise me on my medical condition.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All of us − the children of Mr and Mrs Lee, as well as fellow Singaporeans − share one goal, which is to honour the legacy of Mr and Mrs Lee.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In his Facebook post made this past Saturday evening, Mr Lee Hsien Yang wrote, "I simply hope to ensure our father's wishes are honoured when the day comes." I believe I speak for all Members in this House and many Singaporeans, when I say, we all hope to do the same, to honour Mr Lee's wishes, and furthermore to honour his legacy and the ideals and principles of our founding leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In Mandarin):   By the time I served Mr Lee Kuan Yew as his Principal Private Secretary, Mr Lee was the Senior Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Yet, he continued to devote all his time to thinking about the future of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: His every thought and action was focused on securing Singapore's well-being and success.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If Mr Lee Kuan Yew were still alive, I believe he would want Singapore to remain successful.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: That is why we cannot allow this dispute to sidetrack us from the bigger task of honouring Mr Lee's wish for a successful Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There cannot be a home without a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew devoted his entire life to build a greater house than 38 Oxley Road − and that is Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This house − we cannot allow to be demolished.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us continue to honour Mr Lee's spirit of unwavering dedication, strengthen the foundation of this house and build a better Singapore together.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In English): Madam, I have said earlier, we all wish to honour Mr Lee's wishes and legacy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To do so, it is important to understand what he stood for, what he devoted his life to.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Lee has devoted his entire life to achieving the survival and success of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us not have this difference sidetrack us from the bigger task of honouring Minister Mentor Lee's wish for a successful Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us get back to the business of serving our people.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This house − we cannot allow to be demolished.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: (In Malay):   Please allow me to begin my speech with a poem: Money lost can be regained Wealth cannot be taken to the grave Don't look back in regret When family ties are lost forever During the Parliamentary debates yesterday and today, many questions were posed and explanations given, but I agree that there is still no clear evidence that supports allegations of abuse of power by the Prime Minister or the Government.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: In fact, many felt that we should pay attention to more important issues that affect Singapore, such as the economy, employment and the terrorism threat.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: However, if the serious allegations made by Prime Minister Lee's siblings are not debated and addressed, it will have an impact on Singapore's reputation of having a government that is honest, corruption-free and transparent.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I agree with Dr Janil Puthucheary's view that this sitting is the best platform to give all Members of Parliament an opportunity to ask about matters that Singaporeans would like to know regarding the abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I hope that he realises that this debate would not have taken place if he had not made baseless allegations about the abuse of power by the Prime Minister and the Government.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: During the Lee family's dispute over the past weeks, there was some discomfort when several Ministers made statements on this issue.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Perhaps, can some clarifications be given as to why there is a need for these Ministers to weigh in on this matter?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Why did he not raise this matter before the Probate was issued?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I would also like to seek clarification on why there was a need to form a Ministerial Committee, since we already have a Founders' Memorial Committee.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Why was the Founders' Memorial Committee not asked to give suggestions on the possible options for the house at 38 Oxley Road?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Since its members comprise individuals that can be considered as independent, perhaps this would have been a better approach and the Government could have prevented any negative perceptions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Also, yesterday, after hearing the statement by the Minister for National Development, Mr Lawrence Wong, about the Deed of Gift, I would like to ask a few questions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Were the NHB officers involved unable to exercise good judgement?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: If the NHB officers were instructed to accept the terms, despite their unusual nature, by the Minister-in-charge, this would certainly be considered as an abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: How do our Organs of State ensure that Ministers and other officeholders do not abuse their power?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Do we have a whistle-blowing policy that can take action if there is a case of possible abuse of power by them?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: As my fellow Members have stated, we should pay attention to issues that affect the livelihood, shelter and security of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I think that many are hoping that this dispute can be resolved amicably and the Lee family can begin efforts to reconcile amongst themselves.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I began with a poem and, so, please allow me to end with a poem: Parents lived in harmony Making sacrifices day after day Siblings should never part company But to love each other like a dead knot.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Good afternoon, Mdm Speaker, and good afternoon to all present in the House.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While most of the time, whenever Singapore is mentioned internationally, more often than not, it would have been accolades and achievements rather than negativities.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, this time around, we seem to have attracted international and media attention for the wrong reasons.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: To Mr Prime Minister, I would like to express my regrets on the current situation in which he and his siblings are embroiled in.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am certain no one would like to be in this situation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I wish and hope, through time, that he and his siblings will be able to make amends, re-establish and re-build the family bond, which will be the wish of every parent, even when they have passed on.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to touch on the 38 Oxley Road issue.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: To demolish or not, it has now become a point of contention between the siblings of our Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I have always had the understanding that the late Lee Kuan Yew had always wanted the house at 38 Oxley Road to be demolished, after his and his daughter's passing.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I have always had the understanding that he wished not that the house be turned into a monument and expressed this openly while he was still alive.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Several counter arguments were raised and various ideas were mooted so as to commemorate and make a remembrance of his great contribution to Singapore's success and what Singapore has become today.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Again and again, these suggestions had been rejected by him.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A statement that I could not phrase exactly and that has the message which caught my attention was: "If you wish to remember me and my contribution, just look around you." And I thought this statement encapsulates the spirit and essence of his wish.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The late Lee Kuan Yew's contribution is everywhere around us, not only clean roads, not only green plants and trees, not only modern buildings and first-class economy, but it is more than that.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The late Mr Lee Kuan Yew's contribution to our nation is immense.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: He left behind a system and system of governance which are envied by many nations, big and small.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's achievement from third-world to first-world status is phenomenal.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: He transformed the little red dot into a developed nation with first-class airport, first-class airline, first-class maritime port, high employment and GDP per capita, high literacy rate and many more; a nation based on meritocracy and a champion of corruption-free principles.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty-eight Oxley Road is too small to remember this great man.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I wish that every Singaporean and future ones know what he has done and achieved.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What better way than to instil knowledge into our young and future generations through education in schools.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us invite into our school education curriculum on what the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew wants us to be, based on his principles and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Education should be used as the platform for us to remember and commemorate his contribution.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: From meritocracy to good governance in our institutions, especially Public Service, these are some of the principles and attributes which I believe the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew would want Singapore and Singaporeans to keep and maintain in future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And I sincerely believe this will be more effective and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us leave the decision on the fate of 38 Oxley Road to the family of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like many of us, including myself, we always wish such decision be made private and I hope we can give just that and our respect.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If needed, we may want to consider a replica of 38 Oxley Road on another location, or even a small park as a commemoration.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the issue of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I regard this issue as a serious allegation which we cannot ignore.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Any allegations on our Prime Minister shall not be downplayed, neither should it be dismissed and it must be substantiated with evidence of such.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While this is not evidently clear, I believe it warrants attention based on the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The accusers, Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang are the siblings of the Prime Minister and the children of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our most respected leader in our nation's history.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They hold respected positions in their own field.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They have lived with the system of governance throughout their lives in Singapore, which made them very much aware of the pits and falls of the system.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They must have also understood their late father's views on the principles of the system of governance which has been the hallmark of Singapore's excellence and world-class reputation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They would have also known and able to detect and discern if any abuse of power is exercised by anyone or by any authority.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They would have also understood the seriousness of their allegation which propelled them to bring it into the open, and, lastly, they must also have been aware of the consequence if the allegation made is baseless.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It has tarnished the reputation of Singapore and distracted the Government from far more important work.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Because the allegations against the Prime Minister have been made by members of the Lee family, they are given weight.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: The public is confused and concerned, even as Singaporeans continue to trust the Prime Minister and the Government.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: There is thus an urgency to explain, restore trust and get back on track.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It is our duty and responsibility to do this, to account to our voters.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: My main concern is neither the fate of 38 Oxley Road nor the family feud.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: They are far removed from the daily concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It is the wilful attack on the integrity of our leaders and the insidious erosion of public faith in our institutions that I want to address.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Absent these, Singapore will descend to a Third World country.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Incorruptibility of our Government is what distinguishes Singapore.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: The Prime Minister is central in upholding that incorruptibility.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He holds the key levers of state power, entrusted by the people.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: When trust in the Prime Minister disappears, his moral authority and political capital shrivel.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, the constant self-policing, restraint and care of the Prime Minister in wielding the immense power at his disposal are paramount.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: One's entire character is laid bare and there is only total dedication to the job.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: This is the standard we want to uphold.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: My view remains that when a Minister thinks that an allegation made against him is without basis, he has to sue.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: The Prime Minister has explained in his speech why he would prefer not to sue.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Being the eldest in the family, he must harbour hopes of reconciliation, however remote it seems now, even at a cost to his own political standing.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, I have urged him as well as Lee Hsien Yang to sort out their differences, misunderstanding and reconcile.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It is surely not worth the feud being passed on to the next generation.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Given the immediacy of the issue, I commend the Prime Minister for his courage in opening himself and his Ministers to scrutiny in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Are Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean and the Ministers Prime Minister's puppets?

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: You have listened to Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean's explanation yesterday.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I brought him into politics after he distinguished himself in the Singapore Navy.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He stood with me in the 1992 by-election in Marine Parade GRC.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He went on to serve key appointments with distinction.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Today, he is Minister-in-charge of the Civil Service and Co-ordinating Minister for National Security.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: To suggest that he would do Prime Minister's bidding blindly is to insult the Civil Service and Singapore Armed Forces, never mind the PAP and Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Many of the other Ministers served under Lee Kuan Yew, too.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Lee Kuan Yew told them that he wanted to have his house demolished after his death.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I have come to the conclusion that neither money nor the house is the real issue.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: The dispute over 38 Oxley Road is only a fig leaf for the deep cracks within the family, cracks which perhaps started decades ago.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: What then is the agenda of the Prime Minister's accusers?

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Are they whistleblowing in a noble effort to save Singapore, or waging a personal vendetta without any care for the damage done to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It is now no more a cynical parlour game.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: If the Lee siblings choose to squander the good name and legacy of Lee Kuan Yew and tear their relationship apart, it is tragic but a private family affair.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: But if in the process of their self-destruction, they destroy Singapore too, that is a public affair.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Unsubstantiated accusations have been dished out on Facebook and the media, ad nauseam.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Singaporeans are getting sick and tired of all this.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot, and will not, allow ourselves to be manipulated as pawns.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: There must be a clear conclusion at the end of this debate.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I have heard the Prime Minister's and Deputy Prime Minister's Statements.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I have also been following closely the lengthy postings that Lee Hsien Yang has shared online.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I have known and worked closely with him for more than 30 years.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I brought him into politics in 1984 and, I should add, it was not at Lee Kuan Yew's behest.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He was my Deputy Prime Minister for 14 years.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He has been Prime Minister for some 13 years.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: In this episode, in fact, he has revealed his political sensitivity and integrity.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He gave the proceeds from the sale of 38 Oxley Road away so that no one could accuse him that he would benefit, should the Government acquire the land.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: He had put country before self and family interest.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I still keep a close eye on Government matters.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: This is an occupational hazard for former Prime Ministers.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: The Prime Minister had recused himself a year earlier.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I told Hsien Yang that the dispute over the demolition of the house was actually between him and the Government.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It was not with Hsien Loong, as the Prime Minister has no say over the fate of the house.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I emphasised this point to him − it was between him and the Government.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I agree with Low Thia Khiang that we should end this sad saga and move on.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I have stated clearly my position on the integrity of the Prime Minister and the Government.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: As Prime Minister, I investigated Lee Kuan Yew and Lee Hsien Loong in 1996 over their purchase of apartment units in Nassim Jade.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: My judgement and integrity were at stake then, as today, when I state my conclusion on the Prime Minister's character and integrity.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: I invite Low Thia Kiang and his Workers' Party Members of Parliament, as well as the Nominated Members of Parliament to also state their position clearly on the Prime Minister's and the Government's integrity.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Low Thia Khiang said in his speech, and I quote, that "Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling should not make vague allegations in the public domain against the Prime Minister based on scattered evidence centred on family displeasure.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Making allegations that appear to be calculated to undermine the Prime Minister's authority does not make for constructive politics." Well said.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Follow up with a clear statement of your own that you have come to the conclusion that the allegations are baseless and calculated.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: His colleague Png Eng Huat read out quotes from Wei Ling's and Hsien Yang's 14 June Facebook statement.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: As an hon Member of Parliament, he should state his position on what he has read.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: That is what we are elected as Members of Parliament for − to have a clear view on issues.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: In 1996, at the end of the debate on Nassim Jade, Low Thia Khiang and Chiam See Tong stated their positions unambiguously.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Lastly, if reason fails, I appeal to the emotions and sensibility of the Lees to stop trying to drag each other down and move on.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Stop your family quarrel, sort out any misunderstandings and reconcile, and if that is not immediately possible, at least stop making things worse.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Keep the quarrel private and seek mediation or arbitration to resolve your differences.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: Hsien Loong is here, I hope Wei Ling, Hsien Yang, outside, would hear me, your parents were proud of you.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: This is what your father said during the debate on the Nassim Jade episode: "The proudest thing (for your mother) are her three children − upright, well-behaved and honourable...

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: They are brought up straight, they are likely to stay straight.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: It is like, as I have said, a code of honour.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong (Marine Parade)
text: If you break that code, you have brought shame... upon yourself and family".

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Low, you want to have a word?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong asked us to clarify our position.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We are prepared to give the benefit of doubt to the Prime Minister but we do not know.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I speak for myself because we have not gone through that process.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: For me, personally, I will not be convinced until the entire allegation is given a convincing or conclusive airing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: That means, we should know what else do they have.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I want to clarify on the Emeritus Senior Minister's speech.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: He cited the example of the HPL case.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: And why is this case now different from the HPL case?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I was unaware of any allegation of corruption or wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Thirdly, the subject persons, Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mr Lee Hsien Loong, both father and son, were not Prime Ministers, not the head of the Government at that time.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I wonder how do you convince me, my Party and Singaporeans under the circumstances that this Parliamentary session is conclusive and we all should be convinced, though I said I am prepared to give the benefit of doubt to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But I hope he would clarify some doubts I have on this, nagging question on why he did not sue.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: First, does he not agree that his family is not any ordinary Singapore family and the person at the centre of the issue is the Prime Minister of Singapore, not any other person?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Low, I have given a lot of laxity but clarifications are not a speech, please.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Can you please specify the clarification you wish to seek?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I am seeking clarification arising out of Emeritus Senior Minister's speech because he wanted me to state my position, citing the HPL case and saying why they should not go to the Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But now this allegation is much more serious than that.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: And, more importantly, we are talking about upholding the legacy of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, that the nation, the laws are above family and above individual.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: By using family as justification, does not this show that blood is thicker than water?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: After all, we are all brothers and sisters, but political opponents and critics, sue until your pants drop.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I cannot square, Mdm Speaker, with all these arguments.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong
text: The response by Low Thia Khiang is not unexpected.

speaker: Mr Goh Chok Tong
text: And as for Tang Liang Hong, he is not my brother.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This session was called by the Prime Minister for us to question the allegations and seek clarification.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, when I bring up the allegations, I expect some clarification.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But then, the thing is, it seems that I am not supposed to bring it up because these are issues that are not substantiated.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But these allegations are made by the siblings.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, even when I mentioned that there is a document with Mdm Ho Ching's name listed there as a contact person of Prime Minister's Office, it is an allegation with a documented proof.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am not getting any answers but I am accused of throwing wild allegations at nothing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Today, I heard someone saying, "You may risk contempt of Parliament" because talking about whitewash and cover-up.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, Mdm Speaker, I really do not understand how do these serve the purpose of the Parliamentary session.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: What is your clarification, Mr Low, with regard to Emeritus Senior Minister?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Well, we will proceed to Miss Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was not so long ago that we celebrated SG50, a landmark year for our young nation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: That year, we also witnessed the passing of our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: To say that Mr Lee Kuan Yew played an important role in building Singapore is an understatement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Together with his outstanding team, including Dr Goh Keng Swee, Dr Toh Chin Chye and Mrs Rajaratnam, he laid the foundation for modern Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He gave us values that would make Singapore strong and robust ─ values like taking a long-term view and putting national interest before self-interest, like honesty and integrity, and, most importantly, upholding the rule of law.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He encouraged us to know our past, our humble beginnings and how we got here.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I chose to stay at this house as it holds precious memories and also reminds me of my grandmother's values and struggles in life.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Thirty-eight Oxley Road is not just the house of our founding Prime Minister but also the place where our Pioneer leaders planned the founding of the PAP, Singapore's Independence, fought key general elections and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Part of the Singapore story was written there.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I know there are some who favour demolishing the house, to honour and respect Mr Lee's last wish in his will.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Successive generations of leaders have worked so hard to establish our reputation as a country which upholds the rule of law.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew himself set the example.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am one of those who were inspired by him to be a grassroots volunteer and later to join politics.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I do not fully agree with all Government policies but I believe this is a good Government led by honest leaders and I want to help win as much support as I can.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, the allegations of abuse of power are damaging people's trust and have to be answered fully.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And if the late Mr Lee believed that the house was gazetted, what is going to happen next?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I really hope that this sitting can clear Singaporeans' doubt and restore confidence and they can move on to more pressing national issues.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   The subject of 38 Oxley Road is causing discord in our society.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many elderly residents told me that they hoped we could fulfil the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wish and demolish the house.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, we all know that the biggest wish of Mr Lee was Singapore's prosperity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Thirty-eight Oxley Road has witnessed many historical moments of Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The house has accompanied Mr Lee and the Singapore society through that turbulent era.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Hence, 38 Oxley Road may well represent a spirit which should be passed down to the future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It represents the unwavering spirit and perseverance of the Singapore society.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope we can think it through and do not rush to demolish the house.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Instead, we should first discuss this matter calmly and reach a conclusion afterwards.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After all, once the house is demolished, it can never be reversed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, in March 2015, when news broke of Mr Lee Kuan Yew's passing, the nation reacted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I saw tens of thousands of people queuing to pay their last respects.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Allow me to read one of the notes I came across from a young Singaporean: "Dear Sir, thank you so much for dedicating your life to building this nation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Without you, there wouldn't be a generation of youths like us, and our aspirations to continue bringing our nation to greater progress.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As youths, we will do you proud and not let you down.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Rest in peace." Madam, like this young man, many others ended their notes promising that they will carry on his legacy; they will build a stronger nation, one that he will be proud of.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: That is why we need 38 Oxley Road to remind future generations of what he and his team have gone through, and to inspire them to write the next chapter of our Singapore Story.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe if Mr Lee Kuan Yew were to leave a will for Singapore, his wish would be for our Singapore Story to continue, strong and vibrant, for many generations to come.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have two questions for the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I seek this clarification as I have met and spoken to my residents who live in the Oxley Road area.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them have lived there for decades.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In that same vein, could the Ministerial Committee disclose and provide updates publicly on the options considered and its implications?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The residents of Oxley Road would be directly impacted and thus this concern is raised.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, from time to time, committees are formed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Public opinions these days are aplenty and any position taken will always have opinions for and against it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we continue to uphold the rule of law, how do we ensure that we do not act merely upon public pressure and herd mentality?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Rather, decisions are based on what is the issue at hand and whether it is in the interest of Singapore as a top priority.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, this debate goes beyond the defence of the Organs of the State.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Members in this House and Singaporeans have asked for a quick resolution to this matter.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But we all know that the expectations of reasonable resolution differ from one person to another.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If this situation had happened to an ordinary citizen instead of a high-profile family, do they have any recourse?

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: NHB did not approach Mrs Lee Suet Fern for advice.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: She had reached out to NHB to assist in the negotiations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, NHB thought that, as a board member, she could be useful as an intermediary to reach a satisfactory outcome with the executors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, indeed, she helped to raise some of NHB's concerns with them.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Later, as NHB had to engage in more extensive discussions with the executors to resolve the legal issues, the Chairman of NHB approached her on 12 June to recuse herself on matters concerning the Deed, which she did.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Throughout this process of negotiations, some of the terms were changed over the course of negotiations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But as I said yesterday, the executors held firm to several key conditions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The display of Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wishes in the exhibition, this was something that NHB originally wanted to limit only to the replica of the house that was exhibited.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We see of this now with the benefit of hindsight, but it is important to recognise that, at that time, no one realised that there were these sharp differences of views between the beneficiaries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The assumption was that the executors spoke for all the beneficiaries and these were the firmed conditions set for the donation of the artefacts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, this was my assumption, too, when NHB initially updated me about their discussion with the executors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I only realised that the situation was very different when I spoke with the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under the circumstances, NHB, in fact, considered this matter very carefully.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, several of the objects were in a deteriorated condition and required immediate care and conservation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And third, all things considered, NHB felt that it would be in the public interest to exhibit these artefacts in this major SG50 exhibition.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, Members, with your indulgence, let me just touch briefly on the due process which several Members also spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I have explained, all sites that agencies – be it URA or NHB – have identified with some architectural or heritage merits, go through a rigorous due process.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And there are two parts to this due process.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The first part is the research work which is done internally within the Government and there are various agencies involved in this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The key ones, obviously, are NHB and URA but, depending on the situation, other agencies may be involved like LTA and SLA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The work is done at the staff level but there had been instances where Ministers come together to discuss these proposals which often require inter-agency inputs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After this research work, we may not need to do anything with the property at all unless there is a trigger to take the next step.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This trigger can be by the property owner who submits a development application or it can be by the Government to advance the conservation or preservation proposal.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When that happens, then we move on to the next step, which is to engage the various stakeholders, including experts, relevant advisory panels and boards, as well as the property owner.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And then, after considering all the factors, a decision is made by the Government through the various Ministries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members suggested having more participatory processes to engage and involve the public.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we should not end up with a decision to conserve or preserve a building solely based on a public referendum.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Just looking at the case of Oxley Road as an example, after the publication of "Hard Truths", it appeared that the majority of Singaporeans wanted the house preserved.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After Mr Lee Kuan Yew's passing, the surveys would indicate that the majority wanted the house to be demolished.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The heritage factors are still the same but the opinions have shifted.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, public mood on these matters can shift, depending on circumstances and emotions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am not saying that we should not consult but architectural and heritage merits are careful and rigorous assessments that ought to be done by professionals and subject matter experts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is what we are trying to do − to be ready with all the options, to have drawer plans fully prepared, so that the government of the day is able to make a decision, as and when the time comes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Minister, I would like to clear the air on some of the details.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: There was a time lapse between 8 June 2015 when you updated the Prime Minister on the exhibition and the Deed, and 12 June 2015 where you shared the Deed with the Prime Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Did the Prime Minister ask you for the Deed on 12 June 2015?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If you have initiated the sharing on 12 June 2015, in what context and for what purposes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Because you have already updated the Prime Minister on 8 June 2015.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I related yesterday in my account, NHB and I discussed the matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But when this could not be done – the executors insisted on this exhibition proceeding – we also had to think through what was a possible way to resolve the issues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We had approached the executors to also ask them whether they had the authority to engage in the Deed and if there was consent from all the beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The questions were not fully answered at that stage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But before the questions could be answered, as I related yesterday, they had put out a press statement saying that these were the items that they had donated and this became public information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What is the Ministry's position on the use of the copy of the Deed for personal purposes, no matter how justified, that NHB has given to an officer in his official capacity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I think, more specifically, what is the Minister's response when he came to know after 12 June 2015 that the Prime Minister had used the copy of the Deed of Gift in his personal legal communication with his siblings?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I said that yesterday and I have explained that in the circumstances where there are differences of views amongst beneficiaries – and indeed, where something like this may be contested – NHB would want to share the information with the individuals concerned to make sure that there are non-contesting claims about the artefacts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, while the Deed of Gift was given to the Prime Minister in his official capacity, if he had asked for it in his private capacity, NHB would have shared the information with him, too.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister mentioned that NHB viewed Mrs Lee Suet Fun as a mediator, possibly to assist in the negotiations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Her relationship with the executors would have been a conflict red flag.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Why was it not flagged out earlier that there could be a potential conflict of interest in involving her?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Or was it a case of human lapses?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And how do we prevent, moving forward, instances of civil servants being influenced by persons to allow their involvement?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is it possible for him to share with us how often action was triggered in past cases?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Like I have said, the trigger can be due to a property owner submitting a development application, and, therefore, the Government has to make a decision, either to accept the application or to say, "Look, hold on, because there are these conservation and preservation considerations".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
