text: Alternatively, the Government itself may decide that we want to go ahead and, therefore, we proceed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What URA does is to try to give information to the public.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In its Master Plan, URA would typically highlight some of the potential areas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Which we have identified ahead of time for conservation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is made public in the URA Master Plan.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have had two days of debate on this matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Members from both sides of the House and our Nominated Members of Parliament have asked probing questions, as they should.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, what have we covered in these past two days?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, our rules for avoiding conflict of interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In my Ministerial Statement yesterday, I explained how we maintain separation between private interest and public interest for political appointment holders, as well as public officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is the Code of Conduct for political appointment holders, Rules of Prudence for Members of Parliament from the People's Action Party, and the Public Service Code of Conduct.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Every political appointment holder and public officer is expected, at all times, to act according to the highest standards of probity, accountability, honesty and integrity in the exercise of his public duties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Members of this House know, we treat allegations of misconduct very seriously.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As I said yesterday, there are various avenues for members of the public and public officers themselves, to report suspected misconduct.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If there is specific evidence on the abuse of power by any political appointment holder, public officer, or his or her family members, I can assure you that they will be held to account and the necessary actions taken, if shown to be true.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Public officers are expected to be above board and impartial in their dealings, including with members of the public who happen to be family members of political appointees.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Our senior public officers frequently receive ideas and suggestions from members of the public, including those who may be friends or family members.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have received many suggestions on what I should do about football in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am confident that our senior public officers will go through the due process to evaluate which of these ideas and suggestions are good and useful ones and to put aside those which are unsuitable, regardless of whom these may have come from.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Charles Chong asked about the poll on our public officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As part of regular stakeholder engagement, the Public Service Division (PSD) periodically seeks the sentiments of public officers on issues that matter to them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Public Service will take this opportunity to reinforce in our officers the importance of understanding and living the Public Service Code of Conduct.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore ranks highly on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index for corruption.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Others are watching and evaluating us as we conduct this debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They are watching us to see how we address these allegations of abuse of power and they will see that we are prepared to do so openly in this House, facing the issues directly to clear the air on these issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Prime Minister, myself, the Ministers are held to account by all of you.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Every Member must speak freely in this House and we expect them to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But when a person casts aspersions on the whole of Parliament and its proceedings, and on every one of us, from outside this House − that is a different matter and there are some rules governing this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang, Mr Kok Heng Leun, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Png Eng Huat asked about the appointment of the Attorney-General and Deputy Attorney-General.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There were also questions asked about the role of the Attorney-General and the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law with respect to 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Senior Minister of State Ms Indranee Rajah has comprehensively addressed these issues yesterday and there is no need for me to add anything.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have strict rules on avoiding conflict of interest and they are scrupulously maintained.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, the allegations on the abuse of power.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong has addressed issues related to the Deed of Gift between the executors and the NHB for the purpose of a major exhibition on our founding leaders in September 2015.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: To recap, the Deed of Gift had several unusual conditions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: One of these was the condition requiring the display of one part, but not the whole paragraph, related to Mr Lee's wishes for the house, as stated in his will.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The other was the $1 buy-back clause for the items donated.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These were matters related to a private disagreement at that time regarding the will and how Mr Lee had expressed his wishes regarding the house.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It was a private matter at that time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If NHB is to be faulted for anything, it is that they were drawn, through the Deed of Gift, into this private disagreement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: NHB, a public institution, was being drawn into a private disagreement and the exhibition, a major exhibition, was being used to put out only a part of Mr Lee's wishes on the house.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Members will recall that Mr Lee had said in his will that the whole paragraph could be made public so that his wishes on the matter could be made known.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But to make the display of only one part of the paragraph and not all of it, was drawing NHB, a public agency, and this public exhibition it was organising, into presenting a particular point of view, which was incomplete.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The point I am making is that, contrary to this being an abuse of power, these were efforts to keep NHB, a public agency, and to keep a major public exhibition neutral − to keep them neutral in a matter which was then a private disagreement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is ironical that these efforts to keep our public agencies neutral is now being distorted into allegations of abuse of power for private interests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These are all matters which the Government has to take responsibility for, and must plan for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have also explained why we are starting the process now, to have drawer plans ready, for reference by the Government of the day, when a decision needs to, eventually, be taken.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is nothing unusual or mysterious about it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is just the normal process of Government doing its work, properly, calmly and objectively.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Usually, people will find this quite boring, so there is nothing to get excited about when we formed yet another committee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Instead, it provides coordination and oversight on the matter of 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Ms Chia Yong Yong had said yesterday, it is only appropriate to give due consideration to Mr Lee's wishes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: While at the same time, as the Minister for National Development has just explained, NHB has been documenting the historical significance of the house while MND and URA have been studying options for the property, as well as the planning and zoning implications.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The assessment of buildings of significance is an inter-agency effort, where various Government agencies will do the baseline research.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The establishment of a Ministerial Committee merely seeks to improve coordination and oversight on the matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This also does not preclude the conduct of consultations with heritage professionals and the public at an appropriate stage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Ms Jessica Tan asked why the Ministerial Committee did not reveal its composition earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We could decide to bring in other members as and when needed – the Minister for Transport, for example, when we want to look at traffic issues, or the Minister for Home Affairs when we look at security considerations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang decided to send their representations to the Committee to all the Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Since the Committee reports to the Cabinet less the Prime Minister, there is no issue with this, and they have been doing so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: What was material and relevant had been communicated to them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In any case, should the Cabinet need to make a decision related to this matter, all Cabinet members less the Prime Minister would be involved and collective Cabinet responsibility applies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We should put to rest the allegations about the Committee by Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But before I come to this, let me answer some of the questions that Mr Lim Biow Chuan had.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is proper and correct; the lines are clear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also asked whether we are able to make decisions independently and several Members of Parliament have asked this question as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, as I have said, Madam, we should put to rest the allegations about the Committee by Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Essentially, all the siblings knew about the Committee and what its terms of reference are.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They knew that neither the Committee nor the Government was going to make a decision on the house, as Dr Lee Wei Ling is residing in the house and no decision is needed now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They knew that the Committee was examining a range of options and had no pre-conceived ideas on the outcome.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They also knew that the Committee was not a place where decisions on the legality of the will can be made and this is a matter between the beneficiaries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In fact, they had been making representations to the Committee and sending their representations to Cabinet members at large.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have provided Members with letters and dates to establish these facts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, I will leave it to Members, going through the facts and the chronology, whether there is any basis at all to Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang's claims and allegations about the Committee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is not for me to delve into the motivations behind Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling's allegations of abuse of power over the Committee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But they should not allege abuse of power simply because they were unhappy or felt uncomfortable about being asked to volunteer their views and clarifications on Mr Lee's wishes regarding 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I informed Mr Lee Hsien Yang that I would personally not support the options at either end of the range.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At one end, preserving the house as it is for visitors to enter and see the private spaces.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And at the other end, demolishing the house and putting the property on the market to develop new private residences, such as luxury apartments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang, in his statement on 1 July 2017, stated the same thing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Committee has also been studying various intermediate options and I personally think that there are merits in these intermediate options.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang has, in his public statements, indicated that he is open to some of these options.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is also the position of the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In his statement on 1 July, Mr Lee Hsien Yang said that he also recognised that "no man stands above the law".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, there is no disagreement on this either.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As I have explained, the Government has a duty to go through the due process for when a decision needs to be taken, at some future time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Let us continue doing the work that is needed, calmly and objectively, to study the possible options for the time when a decision has to be made.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As I have said yesterday, I will consult my colleagues to see if it is useful to put out a range of possibilities, to let the public ponder on the matter, without having to arrive at any decision.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But I need to weigh this against arousing emotions again, when what we can really benefit from now is time for calm reflection, especially when no decision is needed now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In summary, the Prime Minister and Ministers have cleared the air and showed that we have acted properly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have described the robust processes we have for Political Appointment Holders, civil servants and Government Members of Parliament to address potential conflicts of interest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We help officers understand and live the Code of Conduct, and we deal with errant officers firmly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This shows that the Government is open and transparent, and accountable for what it does.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This also shows that we have institutions to make sure that we can continue to have good and honest Government in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I hope that these unfounded allegations will stop.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They have no basis and undermine confidence in our system of governance and unfairly tar our public officers who are trying their best to do their duty.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But where do we go from here, as a nation and as a people?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Like many Singaporeans, I am sure that Members of this House have been deeply saddened, shocked and confused by the events of these past three weeks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am certain that Mr and Mrs Lee Kuan Yew would not have wanted this to have happened.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have known Hsien Loong and Hsien Yang for over 40 years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We served together as colleagues and comrades in the Singapore Armed Forces.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have held both of them in high regard for their intellect, objectivity, commitment and dedication to Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Hsien Loong I see now today is the same Hsien Loong I have known all these years − an upright earnest person who stands by his principles and does what is right for Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Ms Sun Xueling, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, others have mentioned, and many Singaporeans know, Hsien Loong has done much for Singapore and he has much more to contribute serving Singapore and Singaporeans as our Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I hope that he will contribute his knowledge and experience to Singapore for a long time to come.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He has contributed much in the Singapore Armed Forces and in the private and public sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have met a number of times since his father passed away.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We spoke to each other with consideration and respect as we always have.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is with deep sadness that the Hsien Yang I see now is not the Hsien Yang that I knew.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I see hurt and strong emotions consuming him.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I do not understand what underlying deep-rooted reasons there may be for this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But for Hsien Yang, I hope that these strong emotions that I see now in his heart will dampen over time and that he would find peace and solace within himself.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He has more to contribute to Singapore if he chooses to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I wish Hsien Yang and his family well, as I always have.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have known Wei Ling also for many years, though not as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: She must have been going through a difficult time over the past few years, living with her parents and looking after them while they were unwell.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And losing both of them, while stoically facing her own health challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I wish her happiness, time to do the things which she enjoys with her friends, now that she has the time and, above all, good health and a long life.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And how much more so it must have been for the immediate members of the family.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When emotions are raw, misunderstandings can arise and feelings can be hurt.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When I met Hsien Yang and Hsien Loong in the weeks after Mr Lee's passing, and Wei Ling a little later, my words to them were "let time pass".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I hope that with the passage of time and the cooling of emotions that the siblings can resolve their private disagreements within the family.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singaporeans, too, can give the Prime Minister and his siblings space to work through their disagreements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng, that all of us, too, in our own way, are also "sons and daughters" of Mr Lee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Lee and his generation of leaders fought hard for all of us and gave us the Singapore we have today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He, and our Pioneers brought us all up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have learnt the lessons that he taught us and which he demonstrated through his own example.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He and his generation built the institutions which uphold these principles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And which we are all proud to call our home.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This episode is a painful one for all of us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But I am confident that this big house we call Singapore will remain strong and robust.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Lee and our Pioneer leaders put in firm foundations − robust processes, institutions and a system of governance which we have continued to strengthen.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Members of this House, Ministers, Prime Minister, our public officers, all Singaporeans − we were all brought up to do our utmost to respect and uphold the values, institutions and processes that are built upon the foundations laid by our founding generation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The moment united all of us, reminded us of who we are and what we stand for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It uplifted us, giving us renewed spirit to face the future together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I hope that as we ponder the options for 38 Oxley Road, and how best to remember the struggles of our Independence years and the values that Mr Lee and our Pioneers passed down to us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This should also be an occasion to unite us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is no reason why this should divide us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Lee, in his wisdom, left us enough room to decide and placed his trust in us to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am confident that all of us, all Members of this House, all Singaporeans, our public officers will build upon the firm foundations of our house, Singapore, and make it even stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is the legacy that Mr Lee and his Pioneer Generation left us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is what they would expect us to do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We can rise above this, we have the confidence and ability to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Let us unite together and fulfil that promise.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Two weeks ago, when I decided to bring this matter to Parliament, I explained my purpose: (a) to air fully all the accusations against me and my government; (b) to allow Members of Parliament to raise difficult and inconvenient questions, whether you are a PAP Member of Parliament, an Opposition Member of Parliament, or a Nominated Member of Parliament; (c) to enable me and my Cabinet to render account to Parliament and clear the air.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In my Ministerial Statement, I have fully addressed the allegations of abuse of power.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In his Ministerial Statement, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean has explained the Ministerial Committee and how we uphold the integrity of the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I brought the matter to Parliament because I am answerable to Members and to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have opened myself up to questioning by Members.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the Members' responsibility to ask me any questions they want and get to the bottom of the issue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, I was surprised that some Members asked me why I had brought this to Parliament and questioned if we should discuss this in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I agree that we should not fight private disputes in Parliament, nor have we done so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But grave accusations of abuse of power have been made against me as Prime Minister and against my government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Doubts have been cast on our Government and the leadership.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How can my Ministers and I not discuss them in Parliament?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Imagine the scandal if Members filed Parliamentary Questions on these accusations and the Government replied that Parliament is not the place to discuss the matter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, whatever else I or the Government may or may not do to deal with this matter, we have to come to Parliament to render account.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, I am glad that in the last two days, we have had a good debate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members, PAP and non-PAP Members have raised questions and my Ministers have answered them and given a proper account.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang talks about "scattered evidence centred on family displeasure".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But he has not accused the Government of anything nor has he given any concrete evidence or cited any.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat read out the litany of allegations by my siblings but he did not endorse them and that is significant.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because it shows that the Government and I have acted properly and with due process and that there is no basis to the allegations of abuse of power made by my siblings, Dr Lee Wei Ling and Mr Lee Hsien Yang.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: My Ministers have, in the course of the debate, dealt with most of the questions and points raised by Members.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thirdly, whether I considered or I am considering the legal options.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and several of her Workers' Party colleagues have raised questions about the propriety of appointing Mr Lucien Wong as Attorney-General (AG) and Mr Hri Kumar as Deputy Attorney-General (DAG).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because Lucien Wong was previously my lawyer and because Hri Kumar was a PAP Member of Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah gave a clear reply yesterday.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is perfectly normal for lawyers to have existing clients and connections and to encounter potential conflicts of interest when they change jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, lawyers with no clients and connections probably have no job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the way to deal with this is also quite standard − for the lawyers to recuse themselves when matters come up which they had previously dealt with in a previous capacity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All professional lawyers know how to handle such matters and every time a lawyer moves from practice unto the Bench to become a judge, the judge has to do the same.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If matters come up which they had previously handled as private lawyers, they just recuse themselves and let others deal with it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And so it is with the dispute with my siblings on the house.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Lucien Wong was my lawyer but now that he is the AG, I have lost a good lawyer.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is not advising me any more on this matter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC), the Government cannot use Lucien Wong either to advise it on this matter because he is conflicted, he used to represent me.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, in this matter, another officer in AGC takes charge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When Lucien Wong's name came up as a candidate to succeed Mr V K Rajah as AG, I endorsed him with confidence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is known as one of Singapore's top lawyers and has a high international reputation, especially in corporate and banking law.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I was even more confident because I had direct personal experience working with him on this case, my personal case.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I had also consulted him informally on Government matters before, when we were working on the Points of Agreement dispute with Malaysia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I knew that he was a very good lawyer.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Everyone involved in the appointment was fully aware that this was the basis on which I was recommending him.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I told them, I told the Cabinet, Lucien is my lawyer, he is a very good lawyer.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the Opposition will make an issue of this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I do not consider this an impediment because there is no difficulty of conflict of interest.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I briefed the President before the matter formally went to him and I told him the same thing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The CPA recommended that he approved the appointment.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And, indeed, after the President approved Lucien Wong's appointment and it was announced, the Law Society welcomed it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Likewise, my direct knowledge of Hri Kumar, as a Member of Parliament and a lawyer, gave me confidence that he would make a good Deputy Attorney General.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I know he has a good legal mind and he has a good heart as a Member of Parliament for people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is critical for Singapore to have a strong AGC and for AGC to have a strong top leadership because the AG is a very important and demanding job, as Workers' Party Members of Parliament have themselves pointed out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is very difficult to find people of the right calibre and range of experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have been involved doing this, looking for suitable people to be Attorneys-General for quite a long time and I have had to do it several times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is important that we get the best that are there to become the Attorney-General.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The role is becoming more complex and we need the most capable people to defend our interests.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You would have thought the matter was settled nine and a half years ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have also outstanding officers within the AGC coming up the ranks and we have promoted them within AGC, we have elevated some of them to the Bench.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, there is the Deputy Attorney-General Mr Lionel Yee, there are two Solicitors-General Mr Kwek Mean Luck and Ms Mavis Chionh, all promoted to their positions recently.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And other career Legal Service officers have been elevated to the Bench to become Judicial Commissioners as a first step, like Pang Khang Chau, Aedit Abdullah, Hoo Sheau Peng and Audrey Lim.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we look for talent and we groom and develop talent within but, at the same time, we seek to reinforce the AGC with lawyers from the private sector because they will both reinforce the team and add to the talent pool, and also, AGC can benefit from their experience with private sector work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have a good team in AGC today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They hold their own with the very best to fight for Singapore's interests abroad.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They pursue cases in Court and handle very complicated cases professionally, competently, where necessary, aggressively.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the appointments of Lucien Wong and Hri Kumar will contribute to building this team and make AGC an even stronger institution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think when the allegation is that you have deceived Mr Lee Kuan Yew and it is directed at the Prime Minister, that can never be a private allegation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has enormous ramifications for my standing and reputation, and the matter has to be answered.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I explained to Members yesterday how my father's primary wish on the house has always been clear − he always wanted it knocked down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Where my siblings and I differ is on whether my father was prepared to consider alternatives should demolition not be possible.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After meeting Cabinet on 21 July 2011, Mr Lee asked me for my view of what the Government would do with the house after he died.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I told him, you have met the Cabinet; you have heard the Ministers' views.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If I chaired the Cabinet meeting, given that these are the views of the Ministers and the public, I think it would be very hard for me to override them and knock the house down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I would have to agree that the house has to be gazetted, to be kept.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if I am not the Prime Minister or if I do not chair the meeting, all the more likely that the house would be gazetted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ho Ching and I knew my father's wishes and also my mother's feelings on the house and we wanted to address their concerns should demolition not be allowed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we came up with a proposal to renovate the house, to change the inside completely, to demolish the private spaces, but keep the historic basement dining room.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And my wife kept the whole family comprehensively informed.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am distributing two family e-mails just to give Members a sense of the conversations and the discussions and how they were conducted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The first e-mail is dated 2 January 2012 and it is from Ho Ching to my father.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, it is to the whole family − Lee Wei Ling, Lee Hsien Yang, Lee Kuan Yew, Lee Hsien Loong, Lee Suet Fern − to keep the whole family informed on what we were doing.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I will just take Members through the beginning and the end.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It says: "Hi Ling, just to update you on one of the ideas for Oxley renewal/development.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As Loong mentioned, the first preference is to demolish the Oxley house and build afresh.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The next best alternative is to renovate and redevelop parts of the house/annex so that it is liveable/rentable for many more years but with a new internal layout.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The renovation renewal idea is to keep or renew the main Oxley house structure, retaining its old world ambience but completely changing the internal layout except for the basement dining room, and redeveloping the back annex into, a two storey annex connected to the main house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Thus, the current private/family living spaces in the main house upstairs will be gone and family privacy protected." And then there is a long description of all the different possibilities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And then we come to the conclusion on the second page: "If there's objection to renting out to, say, expats, then the family could consider moving in at least for the initial years and then Ling can use one of the big bedrooms ... "and so forth where who can go where." Wei Wei (that is the architect) has done various projects including the renewal of Victoria Theatre as well as conservation of private dwellings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As he explained, the conservation requirements typically do not mean preserving the house in its entirety – the interior layouts are often changed to reflect new family usage needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So we have the option of redoing the entire interior layout to remove any linkages back to the private family space.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I give you a second e-mail which is 30 April 2012, that means, about four months later, from my wife Ho Ching to my father, again copied to the whole family, to say that the approvals have been secured and will be delivered to him and please let her know anything else needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And he replied about three hours later, "Noted, nothing to follow up or sign by me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Permission has been granted as I had previously signed in letters to them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Will send them to you." So, you see, it is quite clear, it is quite open, it is not very curt.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The conservation plan was done honestly, transparently and not on false pretences.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because people were then, three weeks after his passing, still very emotional over losing Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Some wanted to honour him by keeping the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Others wanted to honour him by knocking the house down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Whichever decision we made, one way or the other, significant numbers of people would be upset and we are just creating tensions and unhappiness and anxieties for nothing.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Best if we postponed this major decision for a calmer time, let time pass before we come to the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is why I said what I did in Parliament and I see it in no way contradicting my father's wishes or what I had advised my father when he was alive.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Now, many Members have asked me other specific questions on matters after my father died.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Ms Sun Xueling was unsure why I had offered to transfer the house to my sister for $1, but subsequently sold it to Lee Hsien Yang at market value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked why I had not raised matters on the will during probate and why am I expressing concern now and have put my views in the form of statutory declarations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And several Members have suggested that I take legal action to clear my name and put a stop to the matter once and for all.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is a complicated story, but one golden thread running through it right from the beginning is my desire to manage the issue privately, without escalating the temperature and the dispute, and without forcing the issue of my legal rights.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I adopted this approach because it involves family and I was hoping all along to work out an amicable resolution even if that meant compromising some of my own interests.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: She has been living there for some time, in fact, all her life except when she was abroad − small gaps.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And my father had wanted her to continue living in the house after he died if she wished to.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My sister had no objection, so I agreed to this.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings started making allegations about me and escalating them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I told them that they would have to stop attacking me if they wanted the deal done because, otherwise, if I transfer the house to them and the quarrel continues, there is no point.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And they wanted me to give a certain undertaking − I would not go into all the details now − but I could not agree to what they asked for, so we were at an impasse.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We went back and forth for several months.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Every few weeks, my letter would go to them, they would think about it, every few weeks their lawyer would reply to my lawyer.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Faced with these allegations, I reviewed my old family emails.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Kwa Kim Li was my father's lawyer before his last will.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But she sent me and my siblings information about the previous wills of my father and also information about what she knew about the last will.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Only then did I understand what had happened before my father died, and became troubled by how the last will had been done.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I still held back from raising the issues with my siblings, because I still hoped for an amicable settlement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In August 2015, I dissolved Parliament and called the General Election.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings then issued me an ultimatum, to accept their terms by 1 September 2015, which, perhaps coincidentally, was Nomination Day.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They would surely understand that I had many things on my plate and I would respond as soon as the elections were over, which I did.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I could not allow myself, the Government or the PAP to be intimidated by such threats.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I decided to ask my siblings to clarify the circumstances surrounding the last will.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After that, for whatever reason, the 1 September deadline passed uneventfully.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After the election, I again tried to settle the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And then, you do and say what you think fit and I am free to be my own person, I am not constrained in any way.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And I offered this arrangement, which involved the donation to charity, because it was a variation that we had discussed before Mr Lee died, but ultimately had not adopted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, we said, well, if you want to settle the matter, there was this old variation, would you like to take it up now?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Again, I hoped that this would settle the problem and we could keep the matter low-key and, perhaps, gradually subsiding.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Later on, when the Ministerial Committee asked for views from my siblings and me, I wrote in to give my views.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings had put a lot of weight on the first part of the demolition clause in the last will.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That means that if what I had put down is proven to be false, I can go to jail for perjury.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The statements cannot be taken back − they are done, sworn, irrevocable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I did this privately, because it was just to inform the Committee in their deliberations and I did not want to escalate the quarrel.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Unfortunately, at 2.00 am on 14 June this year, my siblings made public allegations against me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I decided to put out the facts and I released a summary of my statutory declarations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Again, in the first instance, I did not take the legal route and sue for defamation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I stand by what I swore in the statutory declarations and published in the statement, but, really, I do not want to go further along this way if I can help it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I did not, and still do not, want to escalate the quarrel.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: At each point, I decided not to try to enforce my full legal rights.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My priority was to resolve the matter privately and avoid a collision.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Some Members still asked why I am not taking legal action against my siblings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For example, Mr Low Thia Khiang advocates my suing my siblings for defamation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This background which I have narrated to Members explains why I have hesitated to do so.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As I said yesterday, I have been advised that I have a strong legal case.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And in normal circumstances, I would surely sue because the accusations of abuse of power are so grave.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But suing my own brother and sister in Court would further besmirch our parents' names.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Low may think that does not count and it is neither here nor there.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Low argued that we should "do whatever it takes to bring the issue to a quick resolution".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But going to Court will not achieve this.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It would drag out the process for years, cause further distress to Singaporeans and distract us from the many urgent issues that we must deal with.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Several Members − Mr Pritam Singh, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Zaqy Mohamad − suggested a Select Committee or a Commission of Inquiry as an alternative.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There are no specifics to the headline charge of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What specifically did I do that was wrong?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And what was wrong with that, whatever that may be?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Workers' Party Members say they are not in a position to judge.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Indeed, Mr Low criticises my siblings for making "vague allegations … based on scattered evidence centred on family displeasure".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If Members believe that something is wrong, it is Members' job to pursue the facts and make these allegations in their own name.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if you think something is wrong, even if you are not fully sure, then come to this House, confront the Government and ask for explanations and answers.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If having heard the Government, you are still not satisfied, then by all means demand a Select Committee or a Commission of Inquiry (COI).

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But do not just repeat allegations and attribute them to others, or ask for a Select Committee or COI because accusations are around, do not know what, but, therefore, we must have a COI to find out what.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But that should not stop Members from talking to them to get their story.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Nor would it stop the accusers from getting in touch with Members, including Opposition Members, to tell their story so that the Members can raise it on their behalf in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is, in fact, how the Member of Parliament system is meant to work.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Those are the Members' duties and that is one reason why Parliamentary Privilege exists.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So that Members, who have heard troubling allegations or news, can make these allegations and raise the matters in the House, even if they are not completely proven and may be defamatory, without fear of being sued for defamation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is how parliaments are supposed to function.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But none of this has happened over the last two days.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: No one says there is evidence of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Even the Opposition is not accusing the Government of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, it is not a case of "oneself defend oneself".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Why do we need in these circumstances a Select Committee or a COI, and drag this out for months?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It will be another Korean drama, full-scale serial.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Should we set up Select Committees to investigate every unsubstantiated allegation, every wild rumour?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As Mr Low Thia Khiang says, "vague allegations".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But until then, let us get back to more important things that we should be working on.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Ministerial Statements and the debate have been important and valuable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Facts and explanations have been put on the record.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Singaporeans have received a full account of how the Government works and what the Government has done in the case of 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I hope that this two-day debate has cleared the air and will calm things down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It would be unrealistic to hope that the matter is now completely put to rest.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not know what further statements or allegations my siblings may make.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But with the benefit of the Statements and debate in Parliament, Singaporeans are now in a better position to judge the facts and see the issue in perspective.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And we can all go back to what we should be focused on and not be distracted from national priorities and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I, too, would like to think this is possible.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It will be a difficult and long road.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I hope that, one day, there will be rapprochement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo reminded us about the national week of mourning when Mr Lee died.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For Singaporeans, who lost their founding father; for my family and for me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For me, the most difficult and emotional moment in that whole week came when I was reading the eulogy at the state funeral service.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When I recounted how, when I was about 13, my father had told me: "If anything happens to me, please take care of your mother, and your younger sister and brother." Singapore was then part of Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We were in a fierce fight with the central government and the communalists.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My father did not tell me, but he knew his life was in danger.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And I thought we had a happy family, and he lived a long and full life.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Little did I expect that after my parents died, these tensions would erupt, with such grievous consequences.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And after so many years, I will be unable to fulfil the role which my father hoped I would.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I hope, one day, these passions will subside and we can begin to reconcile.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: At the very least, I hope that my siblings will not visit their resentments and grievances of one generation upon the next generation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And further, that they do not transmit their enmities and feuds to our children.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am sad that this episode has happened.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I regret that, in addressing public accusations against me, I have had to talk about private family matters in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This is how the system is supposed to work.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When there are questions and doubts about the Government, we bring them out, deal with them openly, and clear the doubts.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If anything is wrong, we must put it right.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If nothing is wrong, we must say so.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong spoke eloquently yesterday of the many issues she felt passionately about, the many challenges we face as a nation, and why we should be focusing on them and not being distracted by this controversy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang called on everyone to focus on rallying Singaporeans to be united in facing the challenges and not be participating in a divisive dispute.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: First, can the Prime Minister confirm that he will sue his siblings in Court or agree to a Select Committee of Parliament if they make more allegations in public?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The second clarification: what are the terms or conditions his siblings wanted on 38 Oxley Road before General Election 2015 which they had threatened to go public with?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As for what the terms were, it is nothing very secret.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Basically, as the discussions proceeded, more and more wild allegations were made against me, including that I was deceiving my father.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, at some point, I said, "No, this cannot continue.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There is no point by selling you the house for $1 and then you keep going around saying that I deceived my father.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They said that, "In that case, you Lee Hsien Loong undertake to help us get the house knocked down and support us having the house knocked down." I said, "I cannot do that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not know what you would do.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not know whether I will agree with everything that you would do.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have already disagreed with you on NHB.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, it is best you do what you want.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have a clarification for Deputy Prime Minister Teo.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I just have one clarification to put to the Deputy Prime Minister regarding his Statement and it is in relation to the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hon Deputy Prime Minister has clarified that the Ministerial Committee operated independently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But would the Deputy Prime Minister acknowledge that there might be a perception that it is not independent by virtue of the structure of the Committee, that the individuals who make up the Committee ultimately do report to an individual with personal ties to the matter at hand even though that is in his individual capacity?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And given that, the risk of that perception seems to have materialised in this case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And given that fact, would a better alternative have been, instead of a Ministerial Committee to look at this, an independent committee outside of the Cabinet where all the members do not report to the Prime Minister to assess it, make a recommendation to the Cabinet, perhaps a public recommendation, and then the Cabinet could still decide and the Cabinet could still own that outcome?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would that not have avoided some of the perceptions associated with the Ministerial Committee?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I have explained, this is no different from the board of a major company − the Member must have represented boards or been on some of the boards.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this is the way we deal with conflicts of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there should be no reason why Mr Leon Perera is unable to understand this, unless he does not want to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I have explained how we do this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are quite capable of acting independently on an issue such as this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Whether we set up another committee, we could end up having a debate on whether this committee actually is independent or not, who are the members, how is it constituted and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And then, eventually, Cabinet still has to decide whether to accept the committee's recommendation or not.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, we still come back to the same issue.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, the important thing here is to know that we have processes in place, that we have honest upright people who can carry through these processes − honestly, independently and promptly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: He said in his statement yesterday, "It is nonsensical to say that because I saw the Deed in my official capacity as Prime Minister, I would not raise the matter with a family member." I am kind of concerned with this statement because I think it blurs the distinction between the public and the private, and I hope that the distinction may be restored.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: First, it seems, from the public exchange, that this was not simply a case when an older brother straightened out his younger brother over coffee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: With all due respect to the Prime Minister, he did not simply raise the matter to Mr Lee Hsien Yang.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: He sent a strongly worded letter of objection through one of the top lawyers in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: And this letter sounds, to the layman at least, for all purposes, like a letter of demand with the implied threats of lawsuits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Does the Prime Minister agree that it is this method that he has used to raise this matter with his younger brother which has given rise to the perceptions and the allegations on the abuse of power?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The second clarification is, I am concerned that what he said will be said as justification for public servants who are acting in the official capacity, coming across information related to their family members doing something wrong and for the public servants then to raise the matter with the family members may possibly alert them to the wrongdoings inadvertently; and, therefore, allowing the family members to try to take actions to avoid legal sanctions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, I hope the Prime Minister could clarify his statement in respect and in relation to the Code of Conduct for public servants and family members.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On the first point, whether I have "lim kopi" with my brother or whether I have sent my lawyer's letter which may be stronger than my kopi-o, I do not think it makes any difference.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This is a concocted objection because I think my siblings did not like the message.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If I am a policeman, I know that there is an investigation against some family members of mine for drugs or money-laundering or something, I have to keep that confidential.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But if it comes to my knowledge that somebody, my wife or my daughter or my son-in-law, went to a Government department and roughed up the place and demanded to be given special attention, or demanded special terms for their deal, then I had better go and tell them straightaway.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I mean, you need commonsense in applying the Code of Conduct but I presume that we will look for commonsense in Ministers and civil servants.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I seek clarification from the Minister for National Development on a related issue.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Am I correct to recall that if a beneficiary were to write in to NHB for a copy of the Deed of Gift, the beneficiary will be entitled to a copy?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, my follow-up point would be that, if in this case, a copy of the Deed of Gift was given to the Prime Minister in his official capacity and then assuming that he took no action on that but he wrote in again, in his personal capacity, as a beneficiary to ask for a copy and he got the same copy of the Deed of Gift, then he could have acted on the second copy, albeit that they are the same.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Am I correct to say that, in this case, there is no practical difference in whether he received one copy or two copies?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Ms Chia, please address the Chair and please ask for permission from the Chair to ask your questions and not engage in a debate with the Minister.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, my question then is: if that were the case, then would it not be no difference whether the Prime Minister received one or two copies?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Prime Minister's speech, the Prime Minister explained that the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew's lawyer was not involved in the last will.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, will the Government or will the Prime Minister, in his private capacity, be pursuing this matter?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: You call that representing the Prime Minister's Office?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: She did not have a business card from the Prime Minister's Office.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Nor do I consider Lee Kuan Yew my father.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I have a question about the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I understand it was set up to look into the public interest aspects of the house.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But what little we heard about what it concerns itself with was what Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wishes were, relating to the house.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Are not these the proper subjects of Mr Lee Kuan Yew's will?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I understand probate was granted − and should not this matter?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For the will is a private matter, as the Prime Minister said just now relating to the seventh version of the will.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: What are the public interest aspects of this will?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am glad that he has stated his position very clearly on this subject.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I took quite a long time to explain the public interest aspects in why we have an interest in wanting to know what Mr Lee's thinking was.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We could have taken quite the opposite view, which is to say, we disregard Mr Lee's view totally, and then, we just decide without taking his view into consideration.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think the Government does that also from time to time, regardless of what personal interests and wishes are.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we felt that, in this case, there was merit in taking Mr Lee Kuan Yew's wishes and understandings and thinking on the matter.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We had communication from him and we had discussions with him, too.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We had a letter which he sent to Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we also wanted to understand what might have been some of his wishes and thinking around some of the possible options that we were considering.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And, hence, we asked the children of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If we wanted to understand his views and we decided not to ask his children, I think that would have been very strange, indeed, and the children would have had a reason to be upset with us − why are you not asking us, why are you ignoring us?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I have explained why and how the issue or subject of the will, how it was interpreted, came up.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling placed a great deal of reliance on it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They were focused on one part of the will but not the other and offered various reasons for it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is how the subject came up, the will itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, we offered each party an opportunity to make clarifications if they wished to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, we asked each party whether they would be alright with letting the other party have a look at the other party's views.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I think that was a very open and transparent process.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I said that clearly several times yesterday, and I said that again today, too.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I hope that, with my saying it one more time, Mr Chen would understand it.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew had said often that Singapore is bigger than himself.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: In this light, I do not consider myself a son of Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: My question is not about why Mr Lee Kuan Yew's private wishes should be taken into consideration but why do we look beyond a will that has been granted probate, that has been proven in Court, for his last wishes relating to the house?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: From all we have heard, that is what the Ministerial Committee concerns itself with.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: And the Prime Minister just now, in his response to questions about what he would do on the will, said it really has no public interest component.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: So, does the Deputy Prime Minister not agree that these enquiries by the Committee beyond the will for clues of Mr Lee's wishes really undermine the work of the probate Court?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Chen, we run the risk of going through the two days' debate all over again about why the issue is placed before Parliament.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: But I shall leave it to Deputy Prime Minister to reply.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But as I have explained, the relevance is there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Certainly, this was not all the Committee was doing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Minister Lawrence Wong has explained what else the Committee was doing, what work the agencies have been doing for the Committee, and we have been considering various things.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this was not all that the Committee was concerned about.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I said so yesterday several times, I said so again today.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I do not think I can be any clearer than that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think the second question is to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have been reading about the confidence in the Government after this whole saga.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think when we talk about confidence, it is not just about what had happened and what had you done.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think what is also important is how do we move on from here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, assuming after today − and I would think we have a feeling that probably more allegations would come − I can imagine then, the Government would start having to deal with these allegations again.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would that not then affect the function of this Government in some way?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, would not having a COI or a Parliamentary Select Committee for the purpose of setting a platform, setting a kind of agenda, as well as deadlines, such that if Mr Lee Hsien Yang and Dr Lee Wei Ling were invited to come for this platform and to make their presentations, whether they refuse or they do, that would actually help us to move on?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The different relevant agencies will come together to discuss this and there have been instances where the discussions have involved the relevant Ministers as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, with Oxley Road, it is a unique case because it is not just about heritage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we have put together this Committee and we are coordinating the work of the agencies.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think it would be very desirable if all the allegations to be made came out in one neat bundle and then we can deal with all of them at once.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There is nothing to stop my siblings or anybody else who wants to accuse me on this subject to hold a press conference, lay out all their facts and information and charges and open themselves to questioning.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If they say more and it becomes necessary, we will consider it very seriously.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And when such a formal forum is convened, I am sure there will be processes to invite, subpoena, produce witnesses, and then to have the matter resolved to the best of our ability.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: What some of the perimeters are, we agree that rule of law needs to apply.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I am actually not quite sure why there is a need for such a furore.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Emeritus Senior Minister Goh alluded to certain things, but that is not for me to know.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I hope that we are able to proceed and let the due process that needs to be taken get on with its work.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I hope that we are able to proceed calmly, objectively in a considered way to do so without all these heightened emotions being involved in this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And at the appropriate time, when we are ready, we will make a decision.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Then, we can consider the matter and decide on the matter.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And if it is useful, without heightening public emotions again, to air some of these, I would consider whether it is appropriate to do so.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, please make it short and quick.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is helpful for us to think about the mood of the day in 1996.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was an editorial in the Straits Times which summed it up quite perfectly actually.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just one line: "More important from the standpoint of a people's faith in their elected leaders and a nation, and its fair system of governance was that the conclusion was reached after an exhaustive process of investigation followed by a full ventilation in the House." The issue here is the accuser − and I am referring to Mr Lee Hsien Yang here − yes, the Minister for Finance is correct, these are accusations, aspersions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He is not just the brother of the Prime Minister; he is a senior member of the establishment, whether we like it or not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: President Scholar, Singapore Armed Forces Scholar, Brigadier-General in the Army, CEO of Singtel, Chairman of the Stock Exchange at one point, Chairman of Republic Polytechnic and a member of the International Advisory Board of Rolls Royce even.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I agree with the Prime Minister that these are just allegations, I am not sure that closure is something that has been achieved in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, my question to the Prime Minister, if these allegations continue, does he not agree that damage would still be done to the Government in some way or another?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think Singaporeans have had a surfeit of news on this subject and I do not think they want more.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If more statements are made, we will have to consider the position.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And I have already explained the circumstances under which we will consider options, whether a Select Committee, a Commission of Inquiry or legal action.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.38 pm until 4.20 pm.
